chunks.text: 12–14 . Given the intricate requirements of the printing process for electronic devices, such as organic light-emitting diodes and thin-film transistors which often involve multi-layered structures, precise control over layer sizes and placements is essential15–17 . Moreover, as electronic devices include diverse materials, the printing process must accommodate inks with varying properties 18 . Among these techniques, the Aerosol Jet Printing (AJP) method has been focused as the most efficient production applied to a roll-to-roll process for large-area electronic circuits and devices. In addition, the AJP technology extends to its ability to generate conductors 12,19,20 , semiconductors 21–23 , and insulators 24–26 , earning recognition as a valuable tool for various applications involving transistors, strain gauges, interconnects, electrode arrays, and more. Aerosol printing stands as a relatively new technique within the domain of printed electronic device manufacturing 27,28 . This method involves the aerosolization of functional ink, propelled by gas streams. Aero- solization is achieved through both pneumatic and ultrasonic means29 . The aerosol stream is directed towards the print head, precisely focused through coaxial sheath gas flow. This process yields a dense deposit of a pre-defined size based on the nozzle dimensions. This paper investigates the process of generating conductive lines through aerosol printing. The fabrication of conductive lines demands adequate thickness for narrow widths and high current-carrying capacity for densely packed circuits. Hence, the aim of printing conductive networks lies in achieving lines with both high resolution (minimal line width) and a substantial aspect ratio (thickness-to-width ratio) 30,31 . However, attaining these objec- tives often poses challenges in maintaining a high printing speed. In the context of aerosol printing, producing a thick line requires multiple processes, ultimately increasing the width of the printed line 32,33 . chunks.text: Materials (KIMM), Daejeon 34103, Republic of Korea. *email: apark@kimm.re.kr -- 1 of 12 -- 2 Vol:.(1234567890) Scientific Reports | (2023) 13:21297 | https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-023-47544-4 www.nature.com/scientificreports/ While most previous research has highlighted the numerical investigation34 and application of aerosol printing for new materials or electronic devices, fewer studies have explored analyzed process conditions that influence print quality at the industrial standard. Firstly, concerning materials, the addition of a surfactant to silver ink increased its electrical property beyond the limitation of the aerosol process 35 . Other cases focus on the aspect ratio of the line pattern achieved by heating the substrate or controlling the operating parameters of aerosol jet printing 36 . However, it is challenging to employ this approach in multi-layer electronic devices due to the high thickness of electrodes, which can render them susceptible to mechanical deformation. Furthermore, the fabrication of electronic devices actively employs aerosol jet technology to enhance performance and simplify processes. A study similar to this paper, involving silver printing through pneumatic aerosol methods, revealed that line width was influenced by three adjustable flow rates and the stage speed of the machine, and the quality of printed line edges changed by manipulating three gas flow rates using pneumatic aerosol equipment 12,32,37 . However, the focus on thickness control primarily revolved around the impact of the deposited layers. Beyond the scope of these studies, the ultimate goal of production equipment is the development of practical processes that can be utilized in the industry. Therefore, the applicability of the pneumatic aerosol jet printing process should be statistically validated. This study aims to comprehensively investigate the interplay between process parameters, such as sheath flow rate, atomizer flow rate, and dispensing speed. Their impact on the morphology and electrical characteristics of lines generated through pneumatic aerosol equipment employing inorganic materials, specifically silver clusters. The optimized conditions yield high-quality line patterns that guarantee resistivity and can be estimated using a regression equation calculated through statistical analysis. Results Fundamentals of aerodynamics in pneumatic aerosol jetting The AJ process employs aerodynamic focusing to achieve high-resolution deposition of colloidal suspensions and/or chemical precursor solutions. An aerosol stream containing the deposition material is meticulously directed, deposited, and structured onto either a planar or a 3D substrate38–40 . This fundamental system comprises two essential components, as demonstrated in Fig. 1: a module responsible for atomizing liquid raw materials (mist generation), and a second module dedicated to focusing the aerosol and depositing the droplets (in-flight processing). The mist generation is accomplished through the utilization of an ultrasonic or pneumatic atomizer. Subsequently, the aerosol stream is precisely concentrated utilizing a flow deposition head, which establishes a circular, coaxial flow between the aerosol stream and a sheath gas stream. This co-axial flow exits the print head via a nozzle directed towards the substrate. The AJ print head exhibits the capability to concentrate an aerosol stream down to a tenth of the size of the nozzle orifice. The system’s distinctive ability to print on non-planar surfaces makes it an optimal solution for producing complicated 3D shape of sensors and displays. This feat is made possible by the relatively substantial stand-off distance (1–5 mm) of the deposition head above the sub- strate, coupled with the extended focal length of the material beam emerging from the nozzle. Notably, there exists no physical contact between any part of the tool (except for the deposition stream) and the substrate, thereby facilitating the achievement of seamless, conformal writing. The AJ printing system consists of three steps as shown in Fig. 1. The first step involves the formation of aerosol in the pneumatic atomizer and its flow through the virtual impactor. The pneumatic atomizer exploits high-velocity gas stream to generate a liquid stream into a droplet size of 1–5 μm. The atomizer connected with add-back module introduces solvent to the atomizer to maintain desired ink viscosity for consistent output. Solvents with low to medium vapor pressure are suitable, but high vapor pressure solvents can lead to excessive drying and powdery deposits. Atomizer flow rate impacts atomization rate, adjustable from 0 to 2000 sccm. Typical rates are 800–1500 sccm, but some materials may need higher rates for acceptable atomization. The optimal atomizer flow rate depends on material viscosity. The second step is a process in which the aerosol stream from the virtual impactor (VI) is filtered to flow smoothly, and excess gas is removed to increase the density of the material. In this step, a solvent add-back mod- ule is used, which adds solvent to sheath gas, saturating atomized aerosol to prevent VI blockage due to drying. The VI sheath flow is set to be the same as the atomizer flow rate. As shown in Eq. (1), the determined flow rate at this point becomes the push flow rate to the deposition head. The third step is the process of printing through the nozzle in the deposition head. Sheath gas flow focuses aerosol mist, defining printed line width. Low flow can reduce product quality; high flow can disrupt printing. Sheath process parameters are often communicated using sheath-to-push ratio, acceptable range depending on nozzle size. The boost and divert flow rates in the deposition head, responsible for redirecting the aerosol stream, will both be set to match twice the selected push flow rate. During process development, the total nozzle flow rate is determined by combining the push and sheath flow rates as shown in Eq. (2). Dispensing height refers to the measurement from the surface of substrate to the nozzle’s tip. Various nozzles necessitate varying dispense heights, with a common guideline being 10 times the nozzle diameter. The pneumatic aerosol printing is influenced by controllable factors: atomizer flow rate, VI sheath flow rate, sheath flow rate, nozzle diameter, dispensing height, dispensing speed, and stage/head temperature. These variables can be categorized into primary variables (atomizer flow rate, VI sheath flow rate, sheath flow rate, dispensing speed) 12,27,32 affecting printability and additional variables (nozzle diameter, dispensing height, stage/ head temperature) 36,42–44 . The primary variables are universal and applicable to a wide range of aerosol jet print- ing systems and additional variables can vary significantly depending on the specific application, materials, and substrates being used. This industrialization strategy enables applicability to all of aerosol jetting equipment. Among the previously defined primary variables, three critical independent factors were selected for conducting factor analysis experiments: (1) sheath flow rate, (2) atomizer flow rate, and (3) dispensing speed. Considering the process parameters, the dependent variables also include the silver ink with suitable properties, along with the dispensing height and stage temperature 28,41 . Influence of critical process parameters in printing quality The aerosol stream is conveyed through a polypropylene tube from the VI to the ceramic deposition nozzle. The ceramic nozzle used has an internal diameter of 300 μm. The deposition head contains nitrogen sheath gas, which aerodynamically focuses or pinches the aerosol stream as it enters the ceramic nozzle. The flow rate of the independent sheath gas can be controlled through a mass flow controller (MFC). The sheath gas is a guiding gas through the nozzle to stabilize the jetting of the ink. By adjusting the amount of sheath gas, the line width and thickness of the pattern can be controlled. Figure 2 illustrates the printed line electrodes based on various sheath flow rates at two different atomizer flow rates of 800 and 1200 sccm. The viscosity of the ink used in experiments is 10 cPs, with further details elaborated in the Methods section below. Due to the variation in the amount of aerosol ejected depending on the atomizer flow rate, it is necessary to set an appropriate sheath flow rate. As the sheath flow rate increases, the ink ejection relatively decreases, leading to a reduction in line width shown in Fig. 2a,b. However, when the sheath flow rate exceeds an appropriate level, the quality of the lines diminishes. The sheath flow rate operates much like when we water a garden using a hose. Just as we gently squeeze the hose’s end to propel the water farther and create a controlled stream, the sheath flow rate concentrates the aerosol to produce fine patterns. However, akin to turning the hose’s nozzle too high, setting the sheath flow rate excessively can have adverse effects, jeopardizing process stability and even leading to short circuits. When the sheath flow rate is 100 sccm, an increase in the atomizer flow rate results in line pattern shorts, indicating that optimizing sheath flow rate is essential for achieving high quality line patterns. Figure 2c,d demonstrated that, at a constant atomizer flow rate of 800 and 1200 sccm, an increase in sheath flow rate led to a decrease in line width and subsequently thickness. The atomizer process occurs within the atomization jar to generate an aerosol stream from the ink. Incoming nitrogen gas carries the mist of fine droplets from the exhaust port of the atomization jar after atomizing the ink. Conversely, larger droplets, due to their significant inertial momentum, remain unaffected by the nitrogen and stay in place. In the case of pneumatic atomization, the aerosol stream is formed by the nitrogen gas flowing verti- cally through the ink, regulated by the atomizer (ATM) flow rate, allowing for precise control over the amount of atomized ink. The atomized stream contains ink droplets, some of which are large enough to potentially clog the nozzle. The virtual impactor sheath (VIS) is positioned behind the atomizer, as depicted in Fig. 1. The VIS includes multiple vacuum inlets that can filter the aerosol stream. Ink droplets with lower inertial momentum, which tend to form satellites during printing, are carried along by the nitrogen gas and subsequently expelled through a filter. From an aerodynamic perspective, particularly in the ink injection system, the eddy shedding, which is the circulation of ink around the substrate, is influenced by the printing frequency and speed 45 . This is the fundamental cause of satellite formation, and when a large number of satellites are produced, they coalesce to make the line width broader and well-defined, whereas a smaller number of satellites result in a satellite state. The F-value is a testing statistic employed in regression analysis to gauge whether the coefficients of independent variables within the regression equation are equal to zero, signifying the degree of their impact on the dependent vari- able. An F-value closer to zero implies diminished impact, while an F-value greater than zero indicates a more pronounced departure from zero. Meanwhile, the P-value measures the likelihood of the F-value approximating zero. A smaller P-value indicates significant impact of independent variables, while a larger P-value suggests their diminished influence on the dependent variable. A conventional significance level of 0.05 is typically employed, signifying a 5% risk of concluding an association when none exists. Considering the necessity for the electrode application, the samples were evaluated across three levels with respect to resistiv- ity. These levels include: (1) ‘high quality,’ characterized by successful resistivity measurement and intact form; (2) ‘low quality,’ characterized by successful resistivity measurement but flawed form; and (3) ‘defect,’ involving resistivity measurement failure. The printing results for each level can be referenced from Fig. 7c. Figure 7a revealed that the significant factors influencing line width are the atomizer and sheath flow rates. Thus, utiliz- ing these two process parameters, the operability window was designed. The ink used in the experiment can be configured by referring to the graph within the range of atomizer flow rates between 800 and 1500 sccm, thereby determining the suitable sheath flow rate. Process feasibility verification for industrial applications Figure 8 presents the results of verifying the process stability to demonstrate the feasibility for industrialization of the aerosol jet process. Since factors that affect production yield largely involve electrode formation, process stability assessment is essential for electrode formation processes. The samples used for evaluation were printed with sheath flow rate of 90 sccm, atomizer flow rate of 800 sccm, and dispensing speed of 5 mm/s. Process stability was defined by evaluating the changes in line width and resistivity values over process time and cycle. Thus, the approach involved printing line patterns every 30 min, measuring the line width and resistivity for 10 patterns each time. Examining the line width results over time in Fig. 8a, it can be observed that the variations for each time point remain within ± 4% based on the measurements of 10 patterns at each time. Furthermore, even as the printing time increases, there is minimal difference in the line width of the printed patterns, staying within ± 5% difference. The resistivity results in Fig. 8b also show a similar tendency, where the measurements for each time period, comprising 10 samples, change within ± 3% variation. The resistivity results in Fig. 8b also show a similar tendency, where the measurements for each time period, comprising 10 samples, change within ± 3% variation. Even with continuous printing over 5 hours, there is no significant difference exceeding ± 4% in the resistivity. Ultimately, compared to commercial inkjet and dispensing processes, aerosol jet printing breaks down any ink into small droplets, reducing the risk of nozzle clogging, thereby ensuring high process stability and the ability to form precise patterns. This high- lights the potential of aerosol jet processes as a highly stable method that can be applied in practical industries. Conclusion This study executed a line pattern process by controlling three parameters: sheath flow rate, atomizer flow rate, and dispensing speed, using a pneumatic aerosol jet printing machine. A systematic investigation of aerosol jet printing process parameters reveals conditions for generating high-quality conductive lines. The study analyzed the influence of adjustable parameters on the aerosol jetting process, based on the quality of printed line patterns and its resistivity. Examination of the printed line shapes indicates that sheath gas and atomizer flow rate sig- nificantly influence line printing quality, while dispensing speed controls the ink quantity per unit area, thereby governing the line width. This tendency remains consistent even when employing different viscosity silver inks and substrates. Additionally, the substrate temperature was verified as an additional parameter to control the line width and droplet diameter, which depends on the evaporation rate of ink and the spread time of printed ink. The statistical factor analysis was conducted to analyze the effects of each factor on line width, employing F-values and P-values, and deriving regression equations to estimate line width. Furthermore, operability win- dows were designed for the two main factors: sheath gas and atomizer flow rate. Building upon the regression equations and operability windows, a system was well established to print high-quality line patterns that meet the desired width conditions. Finally, the stability of the aerosol jet process, which has a substantial impact on production yield, was assessed by measuring changes in line width and resistance with respect to process cycles and time. The factor analysis of the proposed aerosol jet process in this study establishes a database that can be conveniently utilized in the industry, using an optimization approach based on ink viscosity and evaporation rate. Ultimately, pneumatic aerosol jet printing is a highly valuable research domain for the electrode formation process of flexible, rollable, and stretchable components, an area currently seeing significant research interest. chunks.text: range from 1 to 1000 cPs. The ink contains 12% by weight of the silver cluster in a solvent. For each printing run, an atomizer jar was loaded with 8 mL of the ink. Silver line patterns were printed in a single pass using a commercial Aerosol Jet Printer (AEROSOL JET HD, OPTOMEC Inc.). Dry N 2 (HP grade, 99.999%) was used as the carrier and sheath gas. Experiments were conducted with carrier gas and sheath gas flow rates ranging from 400 to 1700 standard cubic centimeters per minute (sccm) and from 10 to 120 sccm, respectively. The flow rate of the virtual impactor exhaust, divert, and boost was set as 0.185 psi, 100 sccm, and 100 sccm. The nozzle was used with a diameter of 300 μm. The atomizer current was kept constant at 0.28 A and the printer stage heater was not used due to the clogging issue. Stage speeds varied from 1 to 10 mm/s. Printing was done both on silicon wafer and polyimide (PI) film. The ink showed good wetting on substrates and hence no surface pretreatment was required. Unless otherwise noted, the results show data of printing on silicon wafers. The printed lines were sintered in a hotplate at 150°C for 5 minutes until the color of the ink changed from transparent to gray. Measurement and characterization The printed line patterns were observed using optical microscopy (VHX-5000, KEYENCE Co., Ltd.) to meas- ure the line width and tendency according to the operating conditions. The magnification was mostly used as 500×, and 1000×. The thickness and cross-sectional area of printed line patterns were characterized by confocal microscopy (VK-X200K, KEYENCE Co., Ltd.) on silicon wafers. The resistance of the line pattern printed length of 1 cm was measured with a precise resolution source meter (2634B, KEITHLEY INSTRUMENTS, Inc.) inside of the probe station (EPS200RF, Cascade Microtech Inc.). The source, and measure function was set to voltage and current, separately. The source mode was DC bias, and the level of voltage was used as 1 V. Ultrasonic troubleshooting ......................................................................................................... 162 -- 12 of 176 -- 9000983 Aerosol Jet HD2™ Process Manual Page 1 Chapter 1 HD2 Process Description Important Thoroughly review this entire manual prior to using the Aerosol Jet HD2 system. 1.1 Printing Process The Aerosol Jet® (AJ) HD2™ system provides the ability to print fine-feature electronic, structural, and biological patterns onto almost any surface, with feature sizes as small as 10 μm. The printing process is noncontact and conformal, allowing for patterning over existing structures, across curved surfaces, and into channels. During the AJ printing process, liquid-source ink is atomized into droplets ranging from 1 μm to 5 μm in diameter. The droplets are entrained in a gas stream and directed into the print head where an annular flow of gas compresses the aerosol stream to a diameter as small as 10 μm. The jet of aerosol droplets exits the print head at high velocity and is deposited onto the target surface (workpiece). The source ink may consist of a combination of liquid chemical precursors, solid particles, and solvents. The AJ system is compatible with a wide variety of inks, pastes, or other materials that can be deposited; including metals, conductors, insulators, ferrites, and polymers. The software interface features complete on-screen control of motion, a vision system for process viewing, and many other tools to aid in the printing and processing of materials. -- 13 of 176 -- 9000983 Aerosol Jet HD2™ Process Manual Page 2 1.2 HD2 Print System The HD2 print subsystem, designed for low-volume production and research printing environments, varies according to the customer requirements and print application. A basic configuration consists of a print head and an ultrasonic and/or pneumatic atomizer. HD2 ultrasonic atomizer cassette The HD2 ultrasonic atomizer cassette (Figure 1) uses an ultrasonic transducer to atomize the liquid source material. The transducer produces high-frequency pressure waves within the coupling fluid reservoir. These pressure waves are transmitted through the coupling fluid (typically water) and into the atomizer vial. Inside the vial, the pressure waves cause the ink or other liquid source material to be atomized, forming small droplets. The atomized droplets are then entrained in a gas stream and delivered to the deposition print head. The ultrasonic atomizer works best for materials with a viscosity in the range of approximately 1 to 10 cP. Inks and materials with high vapor pressures may be used with this method. Particulate suspensions may be atomized with this method, but there is a limit to the particle size that can be contained in a droplet that is ejected from the surface of the fluid. As a general rule, suspended particles should be on the order of 50 nm or less. New materials should be tested on a case-by-case basis. Figure 1. HD2 ultrasonic atomizer cassette, 8003336 -- 14 of 176 -- 9000983 Aerosol Jet HD2™ Process Manual Page 3 HD2 pneumatic atomizer cassette The HD2 pneumatic atomizer (Figure 2) uses a high-velocity gas stream to shear a liquid into small droplets of 1 to 5 μm in diameter. Compressed gas is expanded through the atomizer nozzle, producing a high-velocity jet. As a result, ink is drawn from the reservoir into the atomizer nozzle. Subsequently, the high-velocity gas stream breaks the liquid stream into droplets and suspends them in the flow. Large droplets impact the sidewalls of the atomizer reservoir and drain back into it while smaller particles remain suspended in the gas. Figure 2.

Large droplets impact the sidewalls of the atomizer reservoir and drain back into it while smaller particles remain suspended in the gas. Figure 2. HD2 pneumatic atomizer cassette, 8003334 The gas flow rates necessary to form the high velocity jet are too high to be used with the AJ deposition head and must be reduced. Simply bleeding off gas is inefficient, since atomized material would be lost. Instead, a virtual impactor is used to concentrate the aerosol stream by removing excess atomization gas from the system. The output from the virtual impactor is then directed to the print head. The pneumatic atomizer may be used for inks, pastes, or other materials having a viscosity in the range of approximately 1 to 1000 cP. Particulate suspensions may be atomized using this method. As a general rule, suspended particles should be less than 500 nm in size. Solvents with a low to medium vapor pressure can be used in this system; however, high vapor pressure solvents may exhibit excessive drying and produce a powdery or porous deposit. HD2 Print Head The print head is capable of printing features as small as 10 μm onto virtually any surface. The aerosol stream generated by either type of atomizer is fed into the print head, where it is surrounded by a sheath gas stream that serves to focus and accelerate the aerosol -- 15 of 176 -- 9000983 Aerosol Jet HD2™ Process Manual Page 4 stream, causing it to impact the target workpiece. The sheath stream effect is commonly referred to as aerodynamic focusing. A motorized platen moves the workpiece beneath the nozzle, so that the deposited material can be sprayed onto the workpiece. A process divert is used to interrupt the flow of the focused aerosol stream to pause or stop the printing process. The nozzles for the deposition head are interchangeable. Fine feature nozzles are available in sizes from 100 μm to 300 μm. Wide feature nozzles

Disp message text Conditional Structures IF, END This conditional structure specifies a condition that must be met prior to execution of the commands listed between the IF and END statements. Both statements are required. If the result of the condition when evaluated is True, recipe control will execute the contents within the IF and END statements. If the result of the condition is False, the contents are ignored and recipe execution continues one line beyond the END statement. For example: IF Sheath_PT < 1 WAIT 1000 END WHILE, END This conditional structure specifies a condition that must be met in order to stop execution of the commands listed between the WHILE and END statements. Both statements are required. Recipe control will execute the contents of the structure repeatedly until the condition is evaluated as False. For example: REAL ROW ROW = 0 WHILE ROW < 10 ROW = ROW + 1 WAIT 1000 -- 44 of 176 -- Chapter 2: KEWA Process Control 9000983 Aerosol Jet HD2™ Process Manual Page 33 END LOOP, END This conditional structure can be used either to repeat the contents between the LOOP and END statements for a fixed number of times or until a condition is evaluated as True. Both statements are required. Example 1 (repeats a fixed number of times): REAL ROW ROW = 0 LOOP 10 ROW = ROW + 1 WAIT 1000 END Example 2 (repeats until condition is True): ROW = 0 LOOP ROW < 10 ROW = ROW + 1 WAIT 1000 END Tip Keep things simple. While there are not any specific rules about nesting, other than each conditional structure requires an END statement, it is easy to lose track of what you are trying to accomplish. 2.4.5 External Recipes A recipe can call another recipe from a separate file using the Run_External_Recipe command, followed by a comma and the name of the other recipe file. For example: Run_External_Recipe,MiniValves.ini -- 45 of 176 -- Chapter 2: KEWA Process Control 9000983 Aerosol Jet HD2™ Process Manual Page 34 External recipes can be called as many times as required. When this occurs, recipe control saves the position within the current recipe, opens and executes the external recipe, and then returns to the previous one. Nesting external recipe call sequences is not advised because recipe execution cannot be tracked. When recipe control searches for an external recipe, it executes the first one it finds with a matching filename in the currently-referenced file directory (the directory that was opened for the original recipe). If the file cannot be found in the current directory, recipe control will check all subdirectories. Take care when using multiple recipes with the same name to avoid confusion as to which one is being called and executed. 2.4.6 External Process Control Recipes and process capabilities also can be controlled from other applications. KEWA Process Control can automatically accept commands from any external source connected to the Distributed System Manager (DSM). External control is accomplished by referencing the Process Control Recipe_Out variable. External devices that post commands in the appropriate format to this variable will trigger Process Control to execute the defined command. Note Programming environments outside of LabVIEW and .NET are not supported. Multiple commands are queued in the order they are received, but take care to issue each command separately so that the overall execution is clear. Because multiple sources can issue commands to the same variable, a “fire and forget” approach is best. Such an approach means that the command source does not require and will not wait for any response from KEWA Process Control. If a positive response is required, the external source can continue to monitor the Recipe_Out variable and KEWA Process Control will post an acknowledgment response to the command request. 2.4.7 Closed Loop Control Since recipe

For example, a specific sheath pressure can be maintained by using the recipe to monitor the sheath pressure and dynamically adjust the sheath gas flow to maintain the desired pressure. -- 46 of 176 -- Chapter 2: KEWA Process Control 9000983 Aerosol Jet HD2™ Process Manual Page 35 With this type of recipe approach, system pressure is used to define flow parameters rather than exact values being assigned to the variables. To use this approach, you need to know some starting points to establish atomization and focusing followed by allowing the system to make subtle changes as required. Use this type of control with caution, ensuring that the control is executed more slowly than the pressure response. Like all systems that use closed loop control, if the control responds too quickly, the output can be driven to oscillation. The following example illustrates closed loop control; however, the values are fictitious. To use this type of control for an actual application, the appropriate flows and pressure must be known. As a result, a capillary wave (standing wave–like) structure forms at the liquid interface, with a wavelength related in size to the desired aerosol droplet dimension (3—5 μm). The “crests” of these waves break off to form the aerosol droplets. Ultrasonic atomizers work best for materials with a viscosity in the range of approximately 1cP- 10 cP. They require smaller amounts of material to be atomized compared to the pneumatic atomizer. Inks and materials with high vapor pressures may be used with an ultrasonic atomizer. Particulate suspensions may be atomized with this method, but there is a limit to the particle size that can be contained in a droplet ejected from the surface of the fluid. As a general rule, suspended particles should be on the order of 50 nm or less. New materials should be tested on a case-by-case basis. 4.2 Ultrasonic Components The ultrasonic module system is comprised of the following components: 1. Heat block 2. Ink vial 3. Vial cap 4. Ultrasonic cassette, 8003336 Heat block The heat interface block is responsible for the heat transfer from the heater cartridges into the UA vial. The top portion of the block is where heat is supplied and the bottom portion is where the probe on the UIM is inserted allowing for temperature monitoring. The block contains a small magnet which is used to activate safety switch on the UIM. This is a feature which prevents heat cartridges from being energized when the hardware is not mounted onto the system. The ink vial has a Teflon film mounted to the bottom of the vial which is used to contain the ink and has been designed such that ultrasonic energy is transmitted though the film. The ink vial and the vial bottom are made of anodized aluminum and stainless steel, respectively. Included in the solvent add-back assembly is a bypass orifice that is used to split the incoming dry nitrogen gas. Increasing the size of this orifice will decrease the solvent add-back rate to the atomizer or virtual impactor. Increasing the temperature will increase deposition rate, generally, and effects the ink by decreasing viscosity and decreasing stability. The temperature changes the equilibrium amount of solvents that are contained in the ink and in the gas phase above the ink. If a custom process is developed it is highly recommended that ink temperature be actively measured over a series of runs until ink stability and deposition behavior is well understood. The material temperature can be set by adjusting the atomizer temperature set point, inserting the ink vial into the bath, enabling the atomizer, and waiting about 2 minutes for the temperature to settle. 4.4.3 Sequencing Gas Flows HD2 ultrasonic module sequencing flow procedures help to avoid clogging the nozzle and maintain the highest level of performance, Table 4. KEWA Motion laser controls The laser tool functions in a similar fashion to the deposition head. Selecting the radio button (typically 2: Laser) in the “tool selector” panel of KEWA Motion will offset the coordinate system relative to the alignment camera and enable the generic shuttering functions in VM Tools-generated toolpaths. The tool offset between the laser and the alignment camera can be set in the Tool Manager window using the same automated routine that is used for the deposition head. Instead of printing a crosshair mark, in the case of the laser, a crosshair is etched into a suitable substrate such as burn paper, blue nail polish, or any material that absorbs IR radiation. Once etched, the user aligns the crosshairs in the KEWA Vision alignment camera window. Height calibration of the laser is important to ensure that the focal plane is consistent with the print plane or height of the substrate. The standard bracketry will put the laser focal plane and the print plane at approximately the same height, but further refinement can be achieved by using the laser to etch a series of patterns at varying Z-height. A set of crosshairs or even simple lines can be sufficient for this task. The tool should be lowered to its minimum Z position, and a LOOP

Each loop should step -- 164 of 176 -- 9000983 Aerosol Jet HD2™ Process Manual Page 153 up in the positive Z direction by a small amount, e.g. 0.5-1.0 mm, and this should be repeated over about 5 mm of total Z travel. Use the alignment camera to determine which etched pattern has the minimal linewidth and best edge definition; this is the laser focal plane. Rerun the XYZ tool offset routine at this height to record the proper Z offset. Laser sintering scan speeds may be varied between 1-20 mm/s, although speeds of 5-10 mm/s are most typical. Generally, higher laser power enables faster scan speeds while achieving comparable conductivity to low speed, low power sintering, as seen in Figure 134. Excessively high power can degrade the electrical performance of the printed material, although this is ink dependent. Many silver inks show a partial self-limiting sintering behavior, where the sintered ink becomes largely reflective and does not absorb additional power. Generally, laser sintering is limited to films thinner than 7 μm, although alternating print/sintering steps can be used to achieve higher thicknesses. Drying of deposited ink, either naturally through evaporation or through a lower power laser pass, may be necessary to remove volatile components from the printed material before final laser sintering. chunks.text: REVIEW www.advmattechnol.de Aerosol-Jet Printed Sensors for Environmental, Safety, and Health Monitoring: A Review Christine Fisher,* Lydia N. Skolrood, Kai Li, Pooran C. Joshi, and Tolga Aytug* An emergent direct-write approach, aerosol-jet printing (AJP), is gaining attention for the deployment of rapid and affordable microadditively manufactured energy-efficient sensors and printed electronics. AJP enables a broad range of ink viscosities (0.001–1 Pa s) for printing diverse materials ranging from ceramics and metals to polymers and biological matter. Reproducible, high-spatial-resolution features (≈10 μm), and wide standoff distances (1–11 mm) between the nozzle and the substrate facilitate conformal printing of complex geometrical designs on nonplanar—e.g., stepped or curved—surfaces. This paper aims to provide a comprehensive overview of state-of-the-art AJP-based sensors (e.g., strain and temperature gauges, biosensors, photosensors, humidity and surface acoustic wave sensors, dielectric elastomer actuators, and motion, smoke, and hazardous gas detectors) and to discuss prospective applications. The drive toward cost-effective devices that are smaller, lighter, and better-performing remains a frontier challenge in the field of printed electronics. Consequently, as AJP becomes increasingly utilized in the high-volume manufacturing of miniaturized active and passive sensors, it opens a pathway for facile large-scale fabrication of devices for a wide range of consumer and industrial applications, including transportation, agriculture, infrastructure, aerospace, national defense, and healthcare. 1. Printed electronics, in particular, offer great potential toward re- cyclable and biodegradable solutions in tandem to all their other enabling ben- efits. The ever-increasing proportion of electronic waste has generated cause for alarm, with only ≈25% of e-waste esti- mated to be formally recycled. [1] Com- pared to their traditional counterparts, printed electronics offer several bene- fits, such as minimization of energy con- sumption, attenuated use of hazardous substances, improved recyclability, and efficient use of materials for overall eco- designs. [1] Within the printed electron- ics sector, direct-write methods consti- tute a foremost approach to achieve ad- vanced manufacturing designs. While direct-write techniques were first devel- oped to print conductive circuits based on silver nanoparticle-based inks onto cir- cuit boards, [2] use of these techniques has grown in the scientific community since their induction to encompass a host of free-form deposition methods em- ploying functional[3,4] and structural [5,6] ink formulations on flexible and rigid substrates. Compared to other direct-write additive manufactur- ing (AM) techniques, aerosol-jet printing (AJP) technology has expanded beyond simple electronic circuitry to include actua- tors, sensors, and components used in active and passive wire- less technologies and other microelectronic devices. [7] The his- tory of AJP as a 3D printing technique can be traced back to a gov- ernmental agency Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency- funded Mesoscale Integrated Conformal Electronics project in the late 1990s that was aimed at developing manufacturing pro- cesses with the ability to deposit a range of materials onto virtu- ally any substrate. [8] Since then, AJP has emerged as an advanced manufacturing technique for the design and fabrication of an assortment of diverse sensing modalities. The reader should note that earlier studies often refer to AJP as M 3 D—Maskless Mesoscale Materials Deposition—as Optomec, Inc. originally commercialized the technology before adopting the Aerosol Jet trademark. [9,10] The attributes of direct-write printing have provided ample interest for its ever-increasing utilization in microelectronics fabrication for a highly diverse landscape of applications. Notably, maskless approaches are also better suited for rapid prototyping than traditional methods[11] due to their ability to modify print patterns between runs without incurring costs or manufacturing delays associated with new mask production.[13] AJP offers several distinct advan- tages to the field of microelectronic fabrication (Figure 1). These advantages include the ability to accommodate a wide range of ink viscosities (i.e., 0.001–1 Pa s)[7] and to achieve high-spatial- resolution line widths down to ≈10 μm through fine droplet production, making it an exciting competitor against traditional approaches (Table 2). AJP further enables printed sensors on di- verse substrate materials, including polymers, [14,15] ceramics, [16] and silicon [17] as well as conformal printing on both stepped and curved surfaces. Accordingly, the market for integrating electronics onto and within objects, such as those achievable with AJP, is forecasted to grow to $3.5 billion by 2032.[18] Advances in hardware manufacturing and design, spurred particularly by AM techniques, continuously drive consumers and industry to replace obsolete technologies with smaller, lighter, and better-performing devices. Likewise, biosensors (e.g., antibody detection platforms) and sensing modalities that monitor biologically and physiologically relevant processes (e.g., human activity moni- tors) utilize the advantages of AJP for device miniaturization through printing biocompatible inks for the production of wear- able human performance monitors (HPMs) and cost-effective printed diagnostic assays. The development of AJP-based micro- electronics fabrication for sensing and communication is also a part of an evolution toward the Internet of Things (IoT) and Smart Connected Things (SCoT) for integration into networks of self-automated smart devices that respond in tune with external stimuli and each other.[19–22] Thus, as IoT and SCoT continue to expand and encompass new devices, AJP is applied to broader ar- eas to ultimately drive sensor development and integration with the potential to transform industries’ solutions in the automo- tive, medical, aerospace, and energy sectors. Due to its ability for advanced manufacturing and additive integration of diverse ma- terials, AJP reduces associated costs for IoT-based technologies by 20% over conventional methods. [23] With the fourth industrial revolution (Industry 4.0) underway, IoT-based sensors are not only the central driving force toward next-generation innova- tions, but also encompass broader trends in smart technologies, including smart cities, smart homes, and smart factories. Despite widespread interest in AJP as a greener and a more economical approach, to the best of our knowledge, no comprehensive review of sensors fabricated by AJP exists to date. Brief outlines as part of broader reviews provided by Wilkinson et al. [7] and Huang and Zhu [12] do not include the recent progresses in AJP technologies, and

Working Principle The emergent AJP technique uses atomization and a stream of inert gas to deposit inks as focused aerosol sprays directed toward the printer platen within a wide standoff range (1–11 mm) be- tween the nozzle and substrate. [11,25] Longer standoff distances (i.e., 6–11 mm) can be realized by controlling atomization and gas flow parameters to print conformal patterns onto geomet- rically complex substrates. [26] A schematic of a typical AJP pro- cess is illustrated in Figure 2. Either pneumatic (p-AJP) or ultra- sonic (u-AJP; 1.6-2.4 MHz) atomization can be applied in the AJP process. Both u-AJP and p-AJP modes can produce aerosolized print droplets in the range of 1–5 μm; however, there are sev- eral notable operational differences between these approaches. These differences include the amount of ink volume needed to generate a consistent print stream and additional tooling neces- sary to achieve droplet dispersity/uniformity (i.e., relative distri- bution of droplet size) in the resultant streams. Although p-AJP supports high viscosity inks (≈0.01–1 Pa s), when this mode is employed the monodispersity of the aerosol spray is disrupted, resulting in inconsistent printed features.[7] Hence, to obtain a narrow distribution of droplet sizes a virtual impactor is required for the removal of droplets with insufficient inertia for better substrate impingement (<1 μm) and for those exceeding upper limit for fine printing (>5 μm). [7] Due to this additional require- ment, larger ink volumes are needed for p-AJP than u-AJP.[27] On the other hand, u-AJP, despite its more restricted viscosity range (≈0.001–0.01 Pa s), produces uniform aerosol streams for more reproducible prints at a lower material

[7] Due to this additional require- ment, larger ink volumes are needed for p-AJP than u-AJP.[27] On the other hand, u-AJP, despite its more restricted viscosity range (≈0.001–0.01 Pa s), produces uniform aerosol streams for more reproducible prints at a lower material cost.[7,25] Nonethe- less, the operator must be judicious in selecting deposition flow rates (i.e., atomization strength and aerosol gas flow rate (rate of deposition) and sheath flow rate (printed line width)) where an optimum needs to be established to avoid scatting of weakly bound nanoparticles. [28] Moreover, to avoid clogging of the sys- tem equipment, it is obligatory that the materials of choice nei- ther exceed the upper limit of 2 Pa s nor possess an insufficiently large diameter (<500 nm recommended values). [7,29] Viscosity, surface tension, volatility, density, and other rheological proper- ties of the ink generally determine the parameters for effective aerosolization and printing across different ink types. The reader is directed to several relevant articles for further consideration of the intricacies behind atomization techniques and their re- spective limitations. [7,12,25,30,27,31] Following atomization, the gen- erated aerosol droplets are transferred to the deposition head in a plastic tube by a carrier gas flow, [7] which has been reported to take an average of 10 s to travel this distance. [32] While the droplets are in transport, some collide with the inner walls of the tubing and thus never reach the deposition head.[32] Large and small droplets that in fact reach the deposition head are subject to gravitational settling and diffusion, respectively, and these mech- anisms affect the output of atomized ink. Once the droplets reach the deposition head, the focused stream is accelerated through a nozzle with an internal diameter of 50–300 μm and length of 20 mm. The high build speed of AJP coupled with its ability to support multiple printhead modules enables this technology as a viable candidate for the multilayered, multimaterial deposition of sensors and mi- croelectronics. 3. Enabling Components 3.1. Inks Appropriate ink formulations remain one of the central focuses of AJP research development. Depositions with desirable func- tional characteristics that adhere to conformable morphologies are needed in the pursuit of optimum sensing performances of AJP-based devices (Figure 3b). Producing high-quality prints typ- ically requires optimized process controls based on empirical ob- servations and a considerable understanding of u-AJP and p-AJP atomization techniques, process parameters, and ink rheologies, rather than fundamental principles of aerosol physics or fluid mechanical models.[35] As a consequence, AJP lacks a universal description of the parameters required for jettable ink process- ing, such as the concept of the “Z number” used in IJP. [36] In general, high boiling point/low vapor pressure solvents are em- ployed to ink formulations and dispersed or solvated nanoparti- cles must

chunks.text: As a consequence, AJP lacks a universal description of the parameters required for jettable ink process- ing, such as the concept of the “Z number” used in IJP. [36] In general, high boiling point/low vapor pressure solvents are em- ployed to ink formulations and dispersed or solvated nanoparti- cles must fulfill several parameters: 300–500 nm maximum with <200 nm size preferred; solid content of 5–70% weight; and a shear thinning or Newtonian shear behavior. [37] While most 3D printers specialize in a specific subset of ink classes (e.g., pho- topolymers, thermoplastics, ceramics), any material that can be formulated as a liquid ink (i.e., solvated or dispersed) and pneu- matically or ultrasonically aerosolized is theoretically compati- ble with AJP under the appropriate printing parameters. [7] Thus, AJP-operated ink matrices have included metallic-, resistor-, nonmetallic-conductor-, dielectric-, semiconductor-, adhesive-, resist-, etchant-, and reactive chemistries-based formulations. [37] AJP classically employs silver nanoparticle inks for the depo- sition of lines and conductive traces [2,38] and many such ex- amples can be seen throughout sensor fabrication designs. Although unadulterated silver nanoparticles are a lasting fea- ture of the active material of AJP sensor designs, other nano- geometries such as silver nanowires (AgNWs) [39,40] and metal- lic composites including silver–palladium [41] and silver–carbon nanotubes (CNTs) [42] have been increasingly investigated. Due to their excellent electrical properties, other colloidal metallic nanoparticle systems that have been employed include gold, [43] palladium,[44] and platinum,[45] the latter of which is an emerg- ing ink for high-resolution conductive microstructures that has recently been investigated toward generalizable parameter optimization. [46] While metal nanoparticles can be dispersed into inks using facile methods, their production requires both higher labor and energy input, stabilizers are often required to prevent agglomeration, and postprocessing methods require high temperatures. In the class of metal oxides, several exam- ples have recently appeared: particulate, [47] metal composite, [44] and nanowire-based[48] tin oxides, iron oxides,[49] zinc oxides,[50] and nickel oxides. [51] It is worth noting that superparamag- netic iron oxide-based inks (Fe 3 O4 ) have been recently demon- strated using AJP onto both rigid and flexible platforms to exe- cute movements

[52] Recently, metal hydride-based ma- terials (e.g., titanium hydrides (TiH 2 )) have also been intro- duced as AJP inks. Despite their higher resistivity than silver- and copper-based nanoparticle inks, advantages of corrosion resistance, biocompatibility, improved stability, and versatility can be potentially unlocked for their integration to numerous applications. [53] Carbon nanomaterials likewise remain a pop- ular choice, as carbon inks, [54] graphene,[55] single-walled car- bon nanotubes (SWCNTs),[56] multiwalled carbon nanotubes (MWCNTs), [57] sorted semiconductive derivatives, [58] and metal composites[59] thereof. While carbon nanomaterials used alone perhaps cannot confer the same electrical performances as metallic-based counterparts, they have several advantages when used in conjunction as conductive reinforcements and fillers due to their large surface area and superior mechanical properties; notwithstanding, silver–CNT composite inks have been demon- strated to have considerably lower resistivities than pristine silver inks by functioning as bridges across granular boundaries and defects in the printed lines.[60] Pure graphene inks, in particu- lar, are highly promising materials toward printed sensor elec- trode designs owing to their flexible nature. Point defects that are present within the crystal domain of the graphene lattice provide localized sites of high electrochemical activity for target analytes. To this end, several graphene ink formulations opti- mized for the AJP system have been reported [61–63] with stud- ies noting that graphene/silver composite inks have consider- ably less resistivity than their pure counterparts.[64] Increasingly, polymer-based inks including conducting polyaniline,[65] poly- mer pixels, [66] solid polymer electrolytes (SPEs), [67] and poly(3,4- ethylenedioxythiophene) polystyrene sulfonate (PEDOT:PSS)[68] have also been investigated using the AJP route as active sens- ing materials. A foremost consideration for the formulation of stable polymeric-based inks is the compatibility between the carrier solvent and respective polymer. Note that based on the rule of solubility, chemical species with similar intermolecu- lar forces tend to solvate in each other. (see the Hansen solu- bility parameters for quantification). [36] Notably, polymer-based materials often have lower electrical conductivity than their metallic counterparts in addition to a more challenging pro- duction due to limited stability, solubility, and processability. Recently, new classes of functional materials—ionic liquids, [67] ion gels, [69] MXenes,[70,71] metal–organic frameworks (MOFs),[72] transition metal dichalcogenides, [42,73] and perovskites[74,75] — have also been formulated as AJP inks, further underscoring the versatility of this technology and opening up an unexplored de- sign space for the development of printed sensing devices. In particular, owing to their structural and physical property sim- ilarities to graphene, MXene inks have emerged as a valuable option at a significantly reduced cost. AJP compatible MXene inks were first reported in 2019[76] and the influence of tempera- ture on the resistance characteristics of the printed patterns has recently been investigated. [77,78] Biological ink formulations are likewise a mainstay feature of AJP sensing development, where the printing of macromolecules (e.g., proteins, DNA)[27,79] is an active area of research with studies underway to optimize print- ing parameters. [80] Also of interest are those inks with thermo- electric properties where the thermal energy can be converted to electricity and vice versa, thus enabling a mechanism by which their integration can help to realize self-powered sensing de- vices. Accordingly, using AJP processes, several studies demon- strated maintained thermoelectric properties of such inks follow- ing the printing process. [81–83] All these, and other as-yet to be seen ink formulations highlight the potential for future studies from fundamental physics fluid mechanic modeling to bench-to- manufacturing processing parameters.

Substrates The substrate on which a pattern is printed functions as the base of the AJP sensor and may be attached to larger compo- nents or structures of interest. Alternatively, the materials of in- terest themselves may act as the substrate for an AJP sensor if an insulating layer is used to isolate the print from other con- ductive materials. In general, substrates support AJP designs, separate electronic devices from each other, and form the basis of the electronics package. Traditionally, the substrates of elec- tronics are rigid and physically invariant. With advances in the field of printed electronics, the development of lighter, flexible, and biodegradable substrates has been realized. Some key as- pects when selecting substrates include their shape, intended application, thermal transmittance, mechanical properties, and sintering tolerance. Factors such as ink/substrate compatibil- ity, interaction, adhesion, and wettability all play a role in the resultant print quality and performance of the fabricated de- vice, and so it should be noted that the minimum feature size that AJP can achieve is substrate dependent. For example, fea- tures have been consistently printed at the lower resolution limit (≈10 μm) when employing SiO2 and polyimide (PI) substrates, which are often used in conventional microelectronics and chip fabrication.[37] Moreover, printed patterns generally require a thermal curing step to remove organic solvents and additives used in the ink formulation as well as to sinter deposited ink into a dense and continuous pattern. Printing sensors directly on temperature-sensitive materials for some applications, includ- ing SHM (e.g., poly(vinyl chloride) (PVC) conduit [84] ) or wearable HPMs (e.g., poly(ethylene terephthalate) (PET), [85] polyurethane (PU), [85] and cellulose-based materials[86] ) therefore requires al- ternative strategies to conventional thermal curing methods, as discussed in further detail in the following section. [87] Al- though rigid glass [88–90] and silicon

[87] Al- though rigid glass [88–90] and silicon [40,47,74] substrates are classi- cally employed for a wide range of AJP sensor modalities, flexible substrates including polymers (e.g., polyimide, [65,91,92] PET,[93–95] elastomers[96–98] ), cellulose-based materials[99–101] and even store- bought bandages[102] are being progressively employed (see Fig- ure 3a). For some flexible substrates (e.g., PET), the conformable morphology of these substrates coupled with the ancillary ef- fect of transparency expands applications to future-forward ideas such as electronic skin and smart contact lenses.[103] Moreover, composites of flexible polymers (i.e., polyimide) with classic rigid substrates (i.e., silicon [104] or glass[105] ) have also emerged as hy- brid systems that retain the properties of both materials. Sen- sor integration onto flexible substrates is ever-important for a variety of applications—wearables, portable electronics, health- care devices, and other needs for our increasingly connected so- ciety. For the former—wearables—strips of textiles [20] (i.e., flu- orocarbon, nylon, and polymer fibers) have emerged as viable Adv. Mater. Outside of flexible designs, other interesting sub- strates have emerged such as direct prints onto PVC and acrylonitrile–butadiene–styrene (ABS) pipings[84,106] for direct monitoring of infrastructural strain and fatigue. With respect to SHM applications, authors have demonstrated prints onto car- bon nanomaterial-based substrates including CNT networks [107] and buckypaper. [108] For direct integration onto printed circuit boards and other advanced technological devices, FR4 plastics[109] and prepackaged integrated circuit platforms[110] have been uti- lized. Considering other emerging sensing applications, fully freestanding functional devices [92] have the potential to trans- form the landscape of wearable technologies and other applica- tion areas. Indeed, continued progression of AJP-based devices is expected toward continued miniaturization, increased flexibility, enhanced transparency, and designs that enable self-supported structures. 3.3. Thermal Processing In addition to processing parameters such as sheath flow rate, standoff height, platen temperature, and ink flow rate that af- fect the feature size, electrical properties, and mechanical reli- ability of AJP-produced printed lines, print quality, and hence device performance is also affected by sintering time and tem- perature of nanoparticle-based inks (Figure 3c).[32] As described above, thermal sintering of conductive metallic inks, the conven- tional selection for sensing electrode designs, is required for the removal of excess materials during the sensor fabrication process and ensures the printed line is highly conductive and continu- ous. Following deposition of lines onto the relevant substrate, inks are cured and/or sintered based on the respective prop- erties of the substrate and material type (≈110–300 °C for sil- ver nanoparticle-based inks[85] ) with profiles controlled through specification of the sintering temperature and time. Upon sin- tering, the agglomeration of uniformly stacked metallic nanopar- ticles then partially melts to form a cohesive solid, the process of which affects electrical performance such as resultant line re- sistivity and resistance as well as mechanical performance such as elastic modulus and shear strength of the line. [32] However, it has been demonstrated that lowering the sintering time can de- crease resistance due to attenuation of microcracks in the printed lines.[32] Likewise, resistivity is increased upon lowering sinter- ing temperatures due to increases in porosity caused by infe- rior line melting. While this thermal step does not present a significant issue in applying direct-write techniques to metal [111] or temperature-resistant polymer (i.e., polyimide [112] ) substrates, it poses challenges for materials with glass transition tempera- tures (Tg ) or melting points (Tm ) near or below the ink’s required sintering temperature (e.g., ≈110–300 °C for silver nanoparticle- based inks[85] ). Exceeding the Tg or Tm of the substrate during thermal curing causes the printed device to deform or

Exceeding the Tg or Tm of the substrate during thermal curing causes the printed device to deform or degrade.[85] To overcome these limitations, various low-temperature sinter- ing techniques have been utilized, including laser, light beam, xenon flash lamp, microwave, and electrical sintering. [113] Note that, while these low-temperature alternatives address the issue of damage to the underlying substrate during postprocessing, these techniques can often be nontrivial to apply to complex 3D surfaces. One of the most promising techniques is laser sin- tering in light of its ability to maintain functionality in a 3D space and several examples employing laser sintering applied to AJP-based sensors have been reported. [26,102] As another strat- egy, low-temperature photonic sintering has also been utilized in the fabrication process. [84,86,114] While laser and photonic cur- ing methods can be employed to avoid damage to the underly- ing substrate during postprocessing, these techniques similarly have their limitations—the processing throughput is unsuitable for integration at roll-to-roll and large-area manufacturing levels. To combat this issue, the pulse thermal processing (PTP) tech- nique, which has been demonstrated in inkjet printing, may be used for low-thermal budget, industrially scalable integration of metal patterns onto polymeric, paper, and fabric substrates.[115] The PTP process involves using a xenon flash lamp to deliver short duration, high intensity broadband light to generate the high processing temperatures needed for thin film annealing and recrystallization and compaction. 3.4. For instance, for printed elec- trodes and sensing films structured from graphene-based ma- terials, Raman spectroscopy (a nondestructive technique) has commonly been employed due to its high sensitivity of iden- tifying different carbon structures and phases.[55,116–118] When surface functionalization of graphene is targeted toward the presence of C=O moieties as binding sites, characterization with the surface-sensitive

[45,48,65,88] Surface topography profiles and measurement of the cross-sectional area of printed lines and film thicknesses has been explored through atomic force microscopy.[45,116,119] In addition to sur- face microstructure, both spatial resolution and line conductiv- ity determines the quality of the printed line. Thus, the elec- trical properties of AJP-based sintered printed lines are gener- ally characterized through resistance measurements using a two- [2] or four-point [120] probe method. Parameters including car- rier gas rate, stage speed, and focusing ratio have been demon- strated to affect the resultant resistivity of printed lines using AJP methods. [2] Additionally, in printed silver nanoparticle lines, which represent the most well-studied of all metallic systems, the calculated resistivity is approximately twice that of bulk sil- ver, though some studies have demonstrated approximately equal conductivities. Within wearables, devices as well as in- terconnects must retain functionality under mechanical defor- mation, where the mechanical properties of the device are dic- tated by those of the underlying substrate. Typically, repetitive stretching[92] or bending[69] cycles are performed on the sensor to elucidate how mechanical deformation affects subsequent per- formance, with some studies demonstrating structures that can withstand over 10 000 bending cycles with no noted loss of de- vice performance. [69] It is important to note that both the type of materials used to construct AJP-based sensors as well as the intended sensing mechanisms and properties of the constructed sensor must be taken into account when selecting the most valu- able characterization method. 4. Sensor Types Collectively, printed sensors represent the largest printed elec- tronics market and are expected to grow to $4.9 billion by 2032 due to the rise of many new applications and technologies.[121] When constructing a sensor, some of the basic requirements in- clude its range, accuracy, sensitivity, stability, repeatability, and response time. Overarching fundamental sensing performance, real-world demands of selecting and manufacturing sensors in- clude their cost, size/weight, and power consumptions. Con- sidering the paradigm shift in Industry 4.0 toward large-area IoT-enabled technologies, these requirements are ever more crucial—low-cost, low-power miniaturized sensors are key in the pursuit of a more connected world. Additionally, remaining chal- lenges include densification of integration; cheaper flexible sub- strates; environmental impact of disposability; more economical fabrication processes; and extending the lifetime of devices. [122] For these reasons, direct-write printing has emerged as a vi- able technique toward the manufacture of large-area printed sensors and systems. Although several challenges remain to be overcome, the promise of direct-write methods toward enabling smart sensors and electronics propels their continued develop- ment in the academic and industrial sectors. Their role is so im- portant that flexible printed sensors, generally, are now consid- ered as the

chunks.text: printed sensors and systems. Although several challenges remain to be overcome, the promise of direct-write methods toward enabling smart sensors and electronics propels their continued develop- ment in the academic and industrial sectors. Their role is so im- portant that flexible printed sensors, generally, are now consid- ered as the primary building blocks toward the development of IoT and SCoT due to the unique advantages they confer. Despite the vast amount of research and development across academia and industry, the market for printed electronics remains a “wild west” of endless envisioned applications that have yet to be pin- pointed as the most viable and marketable solutions. Considering the foremost challenges of bench-to-market realization of printed electronics are its materials compatibility and size restrictions, AJP offers a compatible solution toward overcoming these cur- rent roadblocks and printing diverse materials down to low mi- crometer resolutions. Since the early 2000s, AJP has arisen as a complementary technique to IJP and has demonstrated rel- evant applications in printed microelectronics, electrochemical systems, and sensors. AJP is used in diverse applications, such as the low-cost production of strain, gas, biological, photo, and other relevant sensor varieties. In this review, we provide a cat- egorical overview of the history and current status of AJP-based sensing devices, their applications, needs, and future directions. A schematic representation of AJP sensor classes can be seen in Figure 4. 4.1. Strain Sensors Strain gauge devices quantitatively transduce experienced strain or deformations to corresponding changes in resistance, capac- itance, or piezoelectricity. Monitoring strain is essential in non- destructive mechanical testing for SHM, [123] wearable HPMs, [85] smart packaging, [21] and human–machine interfaces.[39] Conven- tional strain gauges are typically composed of a sensitive grid Adv. When strain is applied to the sensitive grid, the original geometry of the foil pattern is distorted resulting in a subsequent change in its electrical resistance.[124] The sensitive grid, which converts sur- face strain of the measured component into a relative change in resistance, is often composed of thin alloy wire or foil traces (e.g., copper–nickel) laid in a meandering pattern and backed by a polyimide, epoxy, or fiber glass reinforced epoxy substrate which is adhered using

chunks.text: sensitive grid, which converts sur- face strain of the measured component into a relative change in resistance, is often composed of thin alloy wire or foil traces (e.g., copper–nickel) laid in a meandering pattern and backed by a polyimide, epoxy, or fiber glass reinforced epoxy substrate which is adhered using cements (e.g., cyanoacrylate, ceramic, cel- lulose nitrate) or epoxy. Notably, such foil-based strain gauges are becoming increasingly obsolete due to their inconvenient size, rigidity, low operating temperatures, and failure under high strain rates. [125] Maintaining strong adhesion between conven- tional strain gauges and structural materials of interest presents challenges for performance. [39] On the other hand, direct-write methods are well-suited to replace conventional sensors as they enable functional material components (e.g., strain gauge pat- terns, insulating backing layers, etc.) to be directly printed onto the structural platform. Additionally, direct-write methods allow for simpler fabrication steps, less toxic waste, and better opti- mal efficiency than fabrication methods for conventional strain gauges, which typically involve mask transfer approaches such as photolithography to pattern the grid onto the substrate. [126] The performance of both conventional and printed strain sen- sors (Table 3), defined as the ratio of relative change in elec- trical resistance to the mechanical strain, is quantitatively ex- pressed as the gauge factor (GF). The GF of AJP-based resistance- based strain gauges (RSGs) is generally higher than conventional foil-based gauges, with some reports finding that they are capa- ble of an order of magnitude larger GF values. [84,102,111,119] Be- sides, AJP is also amenable to generating next-generation strain sensor designs on unconventional substrate platforms, includ- ing complex 3D-printed parts, [26] soft structural textiles, [125] and temperature-sensitive materials, such as PVC conduit[84] and store-bought bandages. [102] In addition to RSGs, recent devel- opments on capacitance- (CSGs) and piezoelectric-based (PSGs) AJP strain sensors for SHM,[125] robotics, [89] and biomedical en- gineering applications[127] are summarized below. Structural Health Monitoring AJP-enabled next-generation conformal microelectronics and SHM sensor designs integrated into IoT-based technologies can reduce downtime and repair costs through fast, location-specific detection of excess strain caused by external forces in diverse systems and structures. [19,123,128] Moreover, because AJP can be used for direct conformal prints onto objects, the technique of- fers greater insights into materials’ performance and failure un- der operation. Hence, AJP has been widely investigated for inte- gration into infrastructural materials. Accordingly, one of the first applications of AJP for the fabrication of strain sensors dates back to 2006 when Honeywell developed a piezoresistive sensor based on metal-doped (m)-polyaniline featuring a GF of 8 that mea- sured pressure via induced strain on a sensing diaphragm.[129] Later, in 2010, Maiwald et al. reported the design of an AJP- based RSG for nondestructive SHM purposes. [111,124] The fab- ricated sensors outperformed the reference foil-based counter- parts (GF ≈3.35 vs ≈1.98) and featured silver nanoparticle ink printed in a meander design between printed polymer encapsu- lation layers which isolate the conductive traces of the RSG from the

[111,124] The fab- ricated sensors outperformed the reference foil-based counter- parts (GF ≈3.35 vs ≈1.98) and featured silver nanoparticle ink printed in a meander design between printed polymer encapsu- lation layers which isolate the conductive traces of the RSG from the underlying metal substrate (Figure 5a). [111] Similarly, Zhao et al. adopted AJP to fabricate composite materials with intrin- sic sensing capabilities.[119] In their investigations, strain sen- sors based on silver nanoparticle-based inks were directly printed onto carbon fiber prepreg, a lightweight structural composite material. The fabricated composites exhibited a GF (≈2.2) com- parable to commercial foil-based RSGs (≈2.1). [130] These early examples showcased AJP as a specialized form of customized 2D printing method and demonstrated its feasibility toward the fabrication of embedded sensors that monitor the mechanical properties of composite structures and for the complete lifecy- cle assessment of structural materials from warehouse to fail- ure. Recently, studies have examined commercial silver nanopar- ticle inks formulated by NovaCentrix, which are uniquely de- signed for AJP and contain a PU adjuvant for improved sub- strate adhesion, which is a common issue for strain gauges. In the investigations by Ratnayake et al., strain gauges are printed onto polyimide substrates and tested on a cantilever beam, dis- playing comparable GFs of 1.74–1.85 to those obtained on com- mercial metal foil-based gauges.[131,132] Applying AJP methods, temperature-sensitive curved material platforms such as PVC conduits equipped with strain sensors have also been fabricated. For example, Borghetti et al. reported printed RSGs on cylin- drical PVC conduits and other plastic platforms for SHM pur- poses (Figure 5b).[84] In this approach, the device was also fab- ricated using a composite ink of silver nanoparticles with a PU adjuvant, manufactured by NovaCentrix. After printing, the ink was cured with a commercial photonic sintering instrument that delivered high-energy pulses of broad-spectrum light for fast and low-temperature curing. [133,134] The AJP sensors on PVC demonstrated an average GF value of 2.42, which is compara- ble to commercial foil-based RSGs. While metallic inks have been extensively used in AJP-based RSGs, carbon-based nano-

While metallic inks have been extensively used in AJP-based RSGs, carbon-based nano- materials offer comparable high sensitivities for strain sensing applications due to their intrinsic piezoresistive properties.[107] For instance, sensors based on CNTs and other carbon-based nanomaterials offer high spatial resolution at the nanoscale with the ability to conform to various structural materials when for- mulated into a compatible dispersion or ink. Thompson and Yoon demonstrated dynamic strain sensors for infrastructure monitoring (e.g., structural vibrations) by patterning MWCNTs directly onto aluminum beams with an insulating cyanoacry- late coating [57] as well as printing a water-based conductive Adv. [135] Li et al. employed me- chanically aligned MWCNT networks, printed silver electrodes, and polyimide substrates to design embedded composite strain sensors with high GFs for engineering applications.[107] Simi- larly, Siddique et al. fabricated embedded strain sensors based on printed silver patterns on MWCNT sheets (e.g., buckypaper) for in situ monitoring of the manufacturing process (i.e., resin flow and degree of curing) in composite structures. It was also reported that these embedded sensors could monitor the struc- tural deformation of composite parts after the manufacturing process. [108] 4.1.2. Sensor-Enabled Smart Objects Smart objects containing sensing components to acquire and communicate relevant information represent another evolving area; thus, direct printing of such components onto geometri- cally challenging objects represents a cutting-edge development in the digital transformation of manufacturing and production in various industrial applications, including healthcare, agriculture, and urban development. [136] Ordinary objects can be transformed into smart objects via incorporating sensors, electronics, and net- work protocols, which in turn can enable data-informed decisions from situational context.[137] As a natural extension, equipping objects with printed strain sensing capabilities has attracted sig- nificant interest from the scientific and industrial communities. For instance,

chunks.text: Ordinary objects can be transformed into smart objects via incorporating sensors, electronics, and net- work protocols, which in turn can enable data-informed decisions from situational context.[137] As a natural extension, equipping objects with printed strain sensing capabilities has attracted sig- nificant interest from the scientific and industrial communities. For instance, Borghetti et al. recently demonstrated a resistive sensing coil and tunable capacitor design using silver-based elec- trodes and polymer-based dielectric/insulating tracks to develop a passive telemetric system for measuring resistive loads. [21] Such passive systems could represent a viable solution for various in- dustrial applications. For example, if integrated into smart pack- aging, this approach can open new avenues by which the food in- dustry can reimagine packing technologies and incorporate mul- tipurpose integrated smart food tags (e.g., humidity, tempera- ture, pressure, gas) for quality assurance and control as well as spoilage detection. While integrated sensors for smart objects are advancing, sensing strain can be challenging on structural or me- chanical parts with complex 3D shapes. Applying conventional RSGs to 3D objects is not ideal considering their limitations on placement due to their size, weight, rigidity, and requirement for planar surface attachments along with wired electronics. [26] On the other hand, recent advances highlight the immense potential of AJP for conformally printing 2D microelectronics and wire- less components onto structural parts with complex shapes while maintaining a small device footprint and lightweight design.[26] Printing onto complex 3D shapes is enabled by the wide stand- off range (1–11 mm) of the focused aerosol ink. Through opti- mizing the printing protocols coupled with the ink rheology, rel- atively large changes in the z-direction during a single pattern- ing run are achievable. [26] Through extending the standoff range, Blumenthal et al. demonstrated that silver-based RSGs, electri- cal contacts pads, and wireless antennas could be printed on a carbon composite material with complex 3D shapes. [26] Follow- ing the printing of an insulating polyimide resin layer, the silver nanoparticle-based circuit pattern (strain gauge and coil antenna) was printed across a 90° bend of the composite part.
