In addition, the same research group fabricated a flexible direct-write pres- sure sensor on a polyimide platform by printing a piezoelectric polymer—poly(vinylidene fluoride)—between two printed elec- trodes (silver and conductive PEDOT:PSS). [26] 4.1.3. Aerospace Applications Sensors fabricated by direct-write methods are well-suited for aerospace applications because of the strict size and weight restrictions imposed on space travel. Technology for these applications is highly contested yet vital in implementing next- generation electronics. Devices that can address critical elements of affordability, scalability, optimization of part performance, and attenuation of manufacturing errors toward the development of aerospace-based composite materials have been widely investi- gated. The effects of space environments on the performance of AJP-based sensors have also been explored. For example, strain sensors can assist the space industry in monitoring the deployment of soft structural textiles used in space missions as inflatable habitats, parachutes, and decelerator systems.[125] In this regard, Fujimoto et al. employed AJP to equip soft structural textiles with flexible CSGs. Investigations involved printing and sintering silver interdigitated electrodes (IDEs) on polyimide substrates, followed by drop-casting poly(methyl methacrylate) (PMMA) as a dielectric material for capacitive strain sensing and finally attaching the sensor to military-grade poly(p-phenylene terephthalamide) (Kevlar) with all-purpose barge cement. In their studies of static, dynamic, and cyclic events, the printed CSGs outperformed commercial RSGs with sensitivity values reaching to GF ≈ 5.2 and capacitance values to 15 nF (Figure 5c). [125] Recently, the same research team also demonstrated a minia- turized Bluetooth-based wireless, multichannel readout system compatible with the developed CSGs for distributed monitoring of soft structural textiles used in space applications. [138] The reader should note that changes in the ambient temperature can affect the performance of strain sensors by thermally induced modulations in the electrical properties of printed traces.[139] To that end, Rahman and others have developed strain gauge sensors with temperature compensation to improve

[138] The reader should note that changes in the ambient temperature can affect the performance of strain sensors by thermally induced modulations in the electrical properties of printed traces.[139] To that end, Rahman and others have developed strain gauge sensors with temperature compensation to improve accuracy during measurements that could have otherwise been overesti- mated by temperature-induced changes in the sensing material’s resistivity. [139–141] These temperature-compensated sensors can be used especially in nuclear reactors and aerospace applications, where exposure to extreme operating conditions is required. In parallel to these developments, space survivability of aerosol printed materials has also been recently explored. Taking into ac- count the dependence of GPS positional data and cell phone com- munications on satellites with rigid electronic platforms, Ouchen et al. evaluated printed silver and gold test structures on ceramic and poly(tetrafluoroethylene)-based substrates in a NASA flight facility to test the effects of atomic oxygen, temperature cycling, and hard vacuum effects over six months of exposure. [142] Their studies suggested that AJP-based structures can be used in space-based environments provided that a protective passivation layer is applied over the printed metal traces. Because of this achievement, AJP-based sensors that are resistant to the effects of space environments could conceivably be employed in integrated sensing platforms to monitor degradation of structural materials under the effects of atomic oxygen and ionizing radiation, such Adv. Human Health Monitoring Gathering precise HPM data can provide key insights into physi- ological information and biomedical metrics that dictate human health, disease, and athletic performance. In the context of tele- health and personalized medicine, a foremost consideration for this application area is the integration of miniaturized sensors into wearable technologies; hence, through its diverse substrate compatibility, AJP has been increasingly investigated as a route toward viable HPM-based devices. To this end, the combination of AJP and photonic sintering has been applied to wearable strain sensors for healthcare applications on temperature-sensitive ma- terials, including store-bought bandages (Figure 6a). [102] Agar- wala et al. demonstrated that strain sensors based on silver nanoparticle inks could be directly patterned onto a bandage ma- terial. In this work, a femtosecond-pulsed laser supplied localized heat to induce sintering while transferring minimal energy to the underlying substrate. AJP has also been applied for healthcare ap- plications to manufacture smart personal protective equipment (PPE).[91] Considering the importance of PPE in the fight against the COVID-19 pandemic, Kim et al. explored the feasibility of AJP sensors for the fabrication of smart medical masks that monitor temperature and strain on the face of healthcare workers.[91] In this investigation, an AJP silver strain sensor onto polyimide was adhered to the flexible portion of the mask near the nose bridge to wirelessly monitor healthcare professionals’ temperature (i.e., irregular respiratory breathing and fever) and strain (e.g., face ir- ritation, bruising) on the face. Recently, stretchable, soft material- enabled miniaturized strain sensors with tunable resistances and GFs (1–7.5) were demonstrated by Herbert et al. (Figure 6b).[39] In this work, AJP is utilized to print polyimide and AgNWs to enable strain sensors that adhere to

Recently, stretchable, soft material- enabled miniaturized strain sensors with tunable resistances and GFs (1–7.5) were demonstrated by Herbert et al. (Figure 6b).[39] In this work, AJP is utilized to print polyimide and AgNWs to enable strain sensors that adhere to conformal surfaces with- out using conventional fixtures. Reusability over ten times was achieved without loss of sensing performance toward monitor- ing human motion and health. In another account, an orthogo- nally assembled hybrid silver nanorod/nanoparticle conductive network is encased in poly(vinyl alcohol) to detect responses to human movement (e.g., joint bending, vocalization) with a re- ported GF of 23. [145] In addition to these developments in AJP- based RSGs, researchers have explored the piezoelectric effect toward strain sensor development. Piezoelectricity, with its abil- ity to convert mechanical energy into electrical signals, is particu- larly promising for self-powered wearable sensor applications. [40] To this end, Fappani et al. measured axial and shear forces by designing a piezoelectric force sensor for applications in SCoT in which a piezoelectric ink is deposited in between two printed parallel bottom silver–palladium electrodes. [41] Notably, as sen- sors continue to decrease in size to fit in smaller and low-power device components, the performance of parallel-plate capacitor designs is limited by their nonlinearity and dependence of ca- pacitance on electrode area. [127] Serpentine, meander, and IDE patterns have been used as alternative designs for capacitance- based shear strain sensing, with simulation studies noting the influence of design parameters such as line width, length, and spacing on sensor performance. [89,146] Du et al. established a tel- lurium and AgNW-based versatile hybrid printing process com- bining AJP and extrusion printing to fabricate stretchable piezo- electric sensors.[40] Furthermore, wearable devices with excellent intrinsic stretchability capable of detecting imperceptible human gestures and pulses were demonstrated, in which the printed Ag- NWs retained both sufficient conductivity and flexibility without a sintering process and did not require sophisticated design con- straints. 4.1.5. Touch Sensors and Robotics Applications AJP has been employed toward biomedical engineering and robotics applications through designs such as capacitance-based force and touch sensors, which are instrumental in bridging the gap between human and machine interaction. Especially, aimed at miniature device applications, IDE designs printed via AJP en- able the fabrication of small footprint capacitive force sensors (i.e., 5 mm width × 30 mm length × 1 mm thickness) that can in fact be embedded in a microfluidic device capable of measuring Adv. [127] In this work, a poly(dimethylsiloxane) (PDMS) microfluidic chip was fabricated with an AJP-assisted method followed by embedding a printed strain sensor, com- prised of a series of silver IDEs and insulating polyimide lay- ers, into the device. This work also involved aerosol deposition of a sodium chloride (NaCl) mold for the microfluidic channel, which facilitated the dimensions of the PDMS chip and embed- ded strain sensor to be perfectly matched. [127] Rahman et al. fab- ricated a capacitive touch sensor using silver IDEs that exhibited technologically relevant capacitance values in the range of 1–5 pF (Figure 5d).[89] Through simulation studies, it was suggested that the device’s sensing performance was relatively insensitive to the electrode thickness, in parallel to observations within an- other simulation-based study.[146] Researchers at Xerox produced a five-point capacitive touch sensor on curved surfaces, including PVC, polycarbonate (PC), and ABS piping fitted with LEDs that denote contact points at the surface (Figure 5e).[106] Outside of touch sensing demonstrations, Wilkinson et al. utilized a hybrid printing process by combining electrohydrodynamic jet printing of a PDMS-based elastomer and AJP graphene platelet ink to develop multimaterial structures toward film-based soft robotic applications. [147] In other work, the same research team designed circular conductive carbon-based ink strain sensors and dielectric elastomer actuators (DEAs) onto commercial acrylic and silicone- based elastomeric substrates for soft robotics applications. [96] DEAs, also known as “artificial muscles,” are comprised of two compliant electrodes with a soft dielectric inner core and are gen- erally employed for robotics actuation. For further robotics ap- plications, several tactile-based sensors have been reported. Re- cently, Wu et al. developed a composite layered device consist- ing of PDMS/BaTiO3 mixture deposited on AJP silver nanopar- ticle electrodes as a soft tactile sensing system that measures capacitive pressure.[148] For pressures less than 1 kPa, the over- laid PDMS/BaTiO3 elastomer structure enhanced the capacitive response of the device by ten times over pure PDMS counter- parts. Sinha et al. designed an ultralow-cost (<$1.5) mechanosen- sory skin-inspired tactile sensor where a piezoresistive pressure sensing element is sandwiched between silver nanoparticle elec- trodes printed on polyimide layers to effectively mimic the epi- dermis, dermis, and hypodermis. [149] The sensing array was as- sembled onto the fingertips of a glove to enable the construction of a smart glove that responded faster than human skin (4 ms vs 30–50 ms) with high sensitivity (1.35 kPa−1 ). In another ac- count, Zhang et al. investigated the potential for integrated tactile sensors onto mechatronic and robotic devices via the simulated design of a silver nanoparticle-based circular-serpentine-pattern strain gauge with a PDMS encapsulation on flexible printed cir- cuit (i.e., polyimide) substrates. [150] Olowo et al. build upon this work by constructing the same circular patterned gauge and uti- lizing a Xenon intense pulse light annealing approach.[120] Olowo et al. also recently applied AJP to deposit a laminated patch of PE- DOT:PSS, a polymer that bestows skin-like sensors with piezore- sistive ability, on top of a constructed robotic skin sensor, demon- strating a reduction in processing time from 5 h to under 30 min.[151] These

However, moving from laboratory demonstrations to real-world products that meet commercially viable performance thresholds, AJP technology needs to overcome specific materials and tech- nology challenges (e.g., integrability, manufacturability, durabil- ity, reliability) associated with the application and type of the device through further advancements in materials and device innovations. 4.2. Gas Sensors Monitoring of specific gases (e.g., NO 2 , NH 3 , H 2 , CO2 ) as key indicators in the domestic and industrial sectors is essential to prevent or reduce adverse effects on the environment and human health. Both 2D and 3D functional materials such as metal oxides, graphene, CNTs, conducting polymers, MOFs, and colloidal metallic nanoparticle systems have been custom- arily adopted as gas sensing materials. [152] While the metal ox- ide class of gas sensors is the most commonly employed sys- tem, their fabrication typically requires the use of complicated lithography or microelectromechanical systems (MEMS) pro- cesses. Furthermore, they must be operated at relatively high temperatures where heaters are necessitated to maintain a par- ticular operating temperature. [153] While other types of systems such as conducting polymers can be manufactured using stan- dard photolithography, direct-write methods stand unparalleled in their simplification of advanced manufacturing processes, especially toward large-area arrays. To this end, miniature gas sensors that encompass lower weight, lower power consump- tion, and that are fabricated at an affordable cost are desired. [154] Such devices can enable real-time continuous monitoring and provide feedback with high temporal and spatial precision. [155] Considering that connected automation and IoT integration is a central focus in Industry 4.0 development, printed gas sens- ing technologies, particularly AJP, have gained importance for the fabrication of microscale devices (Table 4) with such desir- able qualities.

Applications may be found in national defense and nature conservation to personal health monitoring and smart cities [24] as this paradigm supports the practical fabrication of lightweight, portable gas-detecting devices used in tactical mil- itary operations,[65] for explosives and nerve gas detection, [66,109] early detection of refrigerant gas leaks, [65] and early warning sys- tems in the coal mining industry. [117] The performance of gas sensors is based on diverse detection principles including in- direct materials-based solutions and direct spectroscopy; how- ever, a common factor among high-performance gas sensors is a high signal-to-noise ratio in the presence of confounding inter- ferences. Thus, not only is the sensitivity of AJP-based devices important in advancing and unlocking their full potential as ad- ditively manufactured devices, but also the selectivity must be carefully evaluated with respect to other fabrication techniques. Given AJP’s nascent nature in the gas sensing fabrication sec- tor, clearly, more research studies are needed to uncover the gen- eral abilities and performance of such devices. For collective gas sensor types, the following components are integrated to con- struct the final device: gas sensing layer, heater coil, electrode line, tubular ceramic, and electrode. Considering the advantages of AJP in constructing the sensing layer and electrodes at any step of the device integration scheme, unlike monolithic processes, it is noteworthy that several examples have appeared using this technique to fabricate integrated microheaters, as discussed below. Integrated Microheaters There is considerable effort in designing power-efficient mi- croheaters that are central to a range of applications includ- ing portable gas detectors, thermal actuators, microfluidics, and thermal metrology. [156] Traditional hot-plates are ineffective for applications that require portability or remote-location opera- tion; therefore, miniaturization is needed to achieve smaller de- signs that attenuate associated power consumptions and inte- grate well with multiple sensing units.[157] In the

[156] Traditional hot-plates are ineffective for applications that require portability or remote-location opera- tion; therefore, miniaturization is needed to achieve smaller de- signs that attenuate associated power consumptions and inte- grate well with multiple sensing units.[157] In the metal-oxide semiconductor-type gas sensing mechanism, microheaters that enhance the desorption of the target gases and improve the sensing performance of the devices have been customarily adopted. [158] However, achieving a low power consumption and high thermal uniformity remain the main challenges in the fab- rication of such devices. Therefore, optimized microheater de- signs have been actively investigated for gas-sensing applications to provide a low power operation while maintaining high sensitiv- ity and stability. Accordingly, the manufacturing of microheaters requires a delicate balance of geometrical, mechanical, thermal, and electrical specifications. Hence, additive manufacturing ap- proaches such as AJP are considered promising candidates for their fabrication. For example, Arsenov et al. demonstrated fully functional AJP-based platinum microheaters on ceramic sub- strates that exhibited a power consumption of 640 mW at 225 °C (Figure 7a). [159] In the investigations by Khan et al., a Pd-doped tin oxide (SnO2 ) sensor on polyimide substrates is established in which the gold transducer, the microheater, and the electrodes were printed using AJP for CO and NO2 monitoring.[44] In this work, an integrated resistive heater supported operating temper- atures of 250–300 °C at a low power consumption of 78–100 mW. A similar study utilized AJP to produce miniaturized gold mi- croplates on flexible polyimide substrates with an efficient power consumption of 54 mW at 325 °C (Figure 7b). [160] A parallel work included patterning gold-based microhotplates with ultralow power efficient heating (i.e., 12 °C mW−1 ) on double meander 150 × 150 μm 2 heaters.[156] Vasiliev et al. and Samotaev et al. have also been active in employing AJP toward the fabrication of plat- inum microheaters on ceramic membranes to advance MEMS- based sensors. [161–164] Taken together, these studies merit AJP’s feasibility for the fabrication of power-efficient, flexible high- temperature microheaters for practical sensing applications. Adv. Mater.

Detection of Explosive and Fire Related Gases Miniaturized gas sensors featuring user-friendly operations, ease of portability, increased safety measures, and higher sensi- tivities are highly desirable for an IoT-enabled world, and AJP is exceptionally suited for microconformal printing.[41,136] To this end, one of the first all-direct-write gas sensors was constructed by Marinov et al. in 2007 on an FR4 printed circuit board (PCB) to serve as a chemiresistive vapor sensor for military applications. [109] The device was selectively responsive to an organophosphorus nerve gas stimulant, dimethyl methylphos- phonate (DMMP), in the presence of interfering chemicals. In this earlier study, silver IDE lines of 8–10 μm thickness and 20–50 μm width were achieved within the laser micromachined channels of PCBs to demonstrate the proof-of-concept of low-cost radio frequency (RF) identification tags via AJP. Considering the increased security concerns worldwide, such gas sensing devices that can detect low concentrations of nitroaromatic explosives are vital for national security to screen and identify improvised explosives.[165–167] Fluorescent polymers as quenching trans- ducers have been widely explored for this purpose because they offer sensitivity down to parts per trillion in air (i.e., three orders of magnitude higher than the standard bomb-sniffing dog capabilities). [66] Bolse et al. demonstrated the reliability of fluorescence quenching sensor arrays in detecting and discrimi- nating nitroaromatic traces of explosive gases (e.g.,

[66] Bolse et al. demonstrated the reliability of fluorescence quenching sensor arrays in detecting and discrimi- nating nitroaromatic traces of explosive gases (e.g., nitrobenzene, 1,3-dinitrobenzene, and 2,4-dinitrotoluene) with classification accuracy rates of 81–96%.[66,168] This approach involved aerosol- jet printing of commercial conjugated polymer arrays to realize an optoelectronic nose for sensitive and selective trace detection of targeted analytes. AJP printed silver nanoparticle and carbon black electrode structures have also been explored for chemire- sistive sensing of volatile organic compounds (VOCs) onto nanofibrous membranes consisting of poly(acrylonitrile) (PAN) and poly(ethylene terephthalate) (PET) layers.[43] Embedding a thin film of gold nanoparticles as a sensing medium into the 3D, high surface area membrane enhanced sensitivity compared to the reference devices fabricated on conventional non-porous, 2D polyimide substrates. Such flexible paper-based designs are ideal for manufacturing low-cost disposable sensors for human health monitoring applications. Similarly, semiconducting SnO 2 -based sensors have also received considerable attention for defense applications due to their high sensitivities, high thermal stability (i.e., 200–300 °C), and abundant material availability.[48,169] Considering all sensing applications employing metal oxides, SnO2 has received 37% of the research focus.[169] For instance, an aerosol-jet printed SnO 2 sensor on silicon substrates with an integrated microhotplate has been described. [47] While the device exhibited good sensitivity to ethanol and featured ultrafast response time (i.e., 1.2 s), both of which are crucial for effective detection of toxic or explosive gases, the sensing performance was found to strongly depend on the sensing film thickness. Taken together, these recent demonstrations underscore AJP’s print ability with high spatial resolution for rapid prototyping of highly accurate, fast-responding devices for potential applica- tions in national defense. Aside from national security purposes, AJP-based SnO2 devices offer great potential in commercial and residential settings for hazardous smoke detection. Through compact design and the use of low-cost materials, such detectors can also overcome the cost and range challenges associated with conventional smoke detector systems. 4.2.3. Relative Humidity Monitoring relative humidity (R H ) is another highly crucial area for environmental control. Especially, when integrated with other sensors (e.g., temperature) in settings such as hospitals, phar- maceutical compounding centers, residential/commercial build- ings, food processing industries, and agriculture, humidity mon- itoring can improve human health and comfort; contribute to in- creased food safety while reducing waste and health risk; pro- mote crop growth and yield while reducing cost; and extend the lifetime of critical/valuable assets while maximizing their overall efficiency. [170–172] Generally, resistive-type R H sensors are used in residential, domestic, and industrial applications due to their low cost and small footprint. Printing such functional elec- trodes onto challenging 3D structures offers a path toward cus- tomizable application-specific integrated circuits that are com- patible with conventional silicon integration methods and man- ufacturing processes. In this regard, Clifford et al. demonstrated a resistive R H sensor consisting of printed silver nanoparticle IDEs covered with a Nafion film acting as the humidity sensing material (Figure 8b). [110] The printed sensor-on-chip device was constructed directly onto prepackaged silicon components and aimed to provide a solution for joining printed electronics with silicon-based circuits. AJP’s ability for rapid prototyping has also been demonstrated through in situ mixing of inks to create func- tional nanocomposites. Jing et al. created freestanding stretch- able conducting wires from mixtures of polyimide and silver inks capable of functioning as dual strain and humidity sensors (Fig- ure 8c,d). [92] Fabricated devices maintained functionality in the critical range of 0–40% stretching, which is attractive for epider- mal sensing and tactile robotics. Additionally, the sensors dis- played stable performance after repetitive (i.e., >800) stretching cycles. In addition, a flexible R H sensor based on green graphene inks (prepared by triton X-100 dispersant and gelatin binder) was recently fabricated using the AJP process on top of screen-printed carbon electrodes on flexible PET substrates. Sensors showed en- hanced sensitivity with the gelatin modification due to the in- creased hydrophilic sites and exhibited a stable linear response to 30–90% R H across a broad temperature range (22–70 °C). [93] Recently, the direct aerosol-jet printing of an MOF-based mate- rial [Ca(C 4 O4 ) (H 2 O)] (UTSA-280) was demonstrated for the first time, which showed favorable responses to CO 2 gas and R H levels (Figure 8e,f).[72] For agricultural applications, Yin et al. designed dual-purpose soil sensors on polyimide substrates that could de- tect both nitrates and moisture. A silver nanoparticle/iron oxide composite ink overlaid with a protection Nafion film and a sil- ver ink overlaid with an acrylic passivation layer were used as ni- trate and humidity sensing materials, respectively. When placed in sandy soil, the dual printed sensors demonstrated agricultur- ally relevant readings. [49] As the manufacturing demand toward Adv. Mater. [173] 4.2.4. Oxidants and Reductants Sensors that can monitor toxic reducing and oxidizing gases (e.g., NO2 and H 2 O2 ) are needed in various industrial and en- vironmental conditions. As a toxicant, NO2 is regulated under the United States Clean Air Act as a pollutant known to cause harm to human health and the environment, and thus is rou- tinely monitored by governmental agencies.[174] In fact, moni- toring of NO 2 is imperative to counteract environmental pol- lution from industrialization and population growth. Generally, NO2 sensors are used to monitor exhausts emitted from vehi- cles, dangerous off-gases from fossil fuel combustion, pesticide- laced agricultural runoff water, industrial effluent, smog buildup from residential and industrial chimneys, and the exhausts from acid rain precipitates. [175,176] To this end, carbon-based nanoma- terials have shown promise for monitoring NO2 . For instance, Zhou et al. printed chirality-sorted semiconducting SWCNTs as thin-film transistors onto HfO 2 -coated silicon substrates and achieved NO 2 detection down to 60 ppm with enhanced selectiv- ity against other gases (i.e., H 2 and H 2 S) as compared to unsorted SWCNTs. [58] In the work by Kubersky et al., the relationship be- tween different ionic liquids in SPEs and key sensor parameters (sensitivity, response/recovery times, hysteresis, and limit of de- tection (LoD)) were investigated. The group used a ceramic sub- strate with platinum electrodes as a platform to print an aqueous SWCNT ink into a thin carbon-based working electrode (thick- ness 10–20

In addition to NO2 , monitoring of hydro- gen peroxide (H 2 O2 )—a chemical compound used in consumer products, healthcare, food, mining, textiles, and pharmaceutical industries—is also equally important to limit its potential haz- ardous effects. [179] In the investigations by Yang et al., silver mi- croelectrode arrays and UV curable polymer traces with varying pattern dimensions were printed onto glass platforms using AJP and used as electrochemical H2 O2 and glucose sensors. [180] As part of this investigation, array spacing between the electrodes was controlled to evaluate its influence on sensitivity and accu- racy. Results showed optimum performance for 100 μm spaced electrodes, while smaller (30 μm) spaced counterparts suffered from diffusion overlap with neighboring electrodes. Studies on electrochemical transducers functionalized with carbon nanoma- terials (i.e., MWCNTs and graphene) for solution phase H 2 O2 detection have also been performed. While both materials were effective at enriching the electrode–electrolyte interface, results showed that MWCNT-modified electrodes were capable of higher sensitivities (20 μA mm−2 ) than their graphene-modified counter- parts (2.8 μA mm−2 ).[181] 4.2.5. Flammables The versatility of the AJP process has been demonstrated for the development of flammable gas sensing technologies, including hydrogen (H 2 ), hydrogen sulfide (H 2 S), and ammonia (NH 3 ) de- tectors. Due to the heavy use of H 2 across various industrial pro- cesses, the deployment of reliable sensors is vital in maintaining operational safety and minimizing environmental concerns. As a highly abundant compound, H 2 gas is a promising alternative en- ergy source to fossil fuel consumption; however, its flame propa- gation velocity is sufficiently high enough to cause explosions at concentrations as low as 4% by volume in air.[182,183] Therefore, early leak detection systems are crucial. To this end, SWCNT- based H 2 sensors decorated with metal nanoparticles (e.g., Pt, Pd, Au, Ag) promise increased sensitivity, lower detection limits, and faster response and recovery times over traditional metal ox- ide counterparts.[24,184,185] Liu et al. reported an H 2 sensor based on Pt-decorated SWCNTs on silicon substrates fabricated by AJP technology in which the Pt nanoparticles adhered to CNTs cat- alyzed the dissociation process of hydrogen molecules that con- vert Pt into platinum hydride (i.e., PtHx). Platinum hydride in turn bridges electron transfer from the analyte to the CNT layer and changes its electrical properties. [45] In addition, through the nanoparticle-sized droplets generated via AJP, Liu et al. showed suppression of the so-called “coffee ring effect” where dispersed SWCNTs aggregate toward the substrate edges due to capillary flow induced by solvent evaporation, which is well-known to af- fect sensing performance. [45,186] The study reported a low H 2 de- tection limit of 20 ppm through AJP deposition of a uniform network of homogenously dispersed Pt-decorated nanotubes. The printed sensors employed sorted semiconducting SWCNTs, printed ion gels and carboxyl- functionalized SWCNTs as channel materials, dielectric layers, and printed, drain, source, and side-gate electrodes, where the enhanced performance toward NH 3 was attained through ionic liquid-based NH 3 enrichment within ion gels combined with a TFT signal amplification effects. [69] Sensing developments con- cerning vapors of NH 3 and ammonium hydroxide (NH 4 OH) for food safety applications have also recently appeared. Through exploiting the inherent hygroscopic properties of cellulose and combining AJP-based interdigitated carbon electrodes (sensing area of 150 mm 2 ) with flash lamp annealing processes, Cantù et al. created paper-based gas sensors that responded to so- lutions NH4 OH, a critical additive to preserve food safety. [114] Following a similar AJP/flash lamp annealing approach, the group also assembled a prototype paper-based smart food pack- ing sensor. [100] In a humid environment, ammonia dissociates into NH 4+ and OH− ions, which changes the ionic conductiv- ity of the medium and hence the impedance of the paper for detection. 4.3. Biosensing and Healthcare Applications Biosensors that are reliable, disposable, user-friendly, and fabri- cated with facile manufacturing methods are in high demand to address the monitoring and progression of disease, protect human health and safety, and fight against present and future emerging pandemics. Biological sensors enable the transforma- tion of chemical information from biological analytes’ concen- trations into an electrical signal or other analytical signal for external detection. Generally, there are

Biological sensors enable the transforma- tion of chemical information from biological analytes’ concen- trations into an electrical signal or other analytical signal for external detection. Generally, there are three main thrusts for biosensor development—biocatalytic (e.g., enzyme); immuno- logical (e.g., antibodies); and nucleic acid (e.g., DNA). Biosen- sors are composed of four fundamental components: a sensing element/receptor that binds the target analyte; an interface to provide a working environment for biological sensor elements; a traducer to transform physical and/or chemical information from the interaction between the sensing element and analyte into useful analytical signals; and a series of electronic equip- ment such as signal processing, signal amplification, and inter- face circuit. [190] While the traditional method toward fabricating biosensors is screen printing electrodes, [191] this approach natu- rally limits the resultant size of the produced device. Thus, AJP has been applied to unlock miniaturized devices capable of con- tinuous real-time monitoring of biological phenomena. The bio- logical applications of AJP date back to the early 2000s when man- ufacturer Optomec filed a patent application for the aerosolized delivery of bioinks. [192] Since then, the use of AJP in biologi- cally relevant approaches has risen significantly (Table 5) and be- come one of the most active areas of interest in sensor develop- ment. The diversity of materials required to fabricate a biosen- sor reflects the diversity of the human body. Some of the most commonly encountered materials used in the fabrication of ac- tive components under AJP processes include metallic nanopar- ticles such as silver, [104] gold,[88] or metal oxides, [193] carbon nano- materials such as SWCNTs, [56] MWCNTs,[194] and graphene, [195] as well as conducting polymers. [196] Aside from rapid diagnos- tic tools such as the COVID-19 antibody detector,[88] AJP-based biosensors are used for the fabrication of in vitro assays, [27] mimicking cell environments for high-throughput pharmaceu- tical drug screenings, [197] as well as the printing of biological inks for precise tissue engineering. [27] Because u-AJP uses considerably less material than p-AJP, retaining biofunctionality in bioinks comparable to IJP of- fers promise toward the development of cost-effective in vitro di- agnostic assays.[27] Another recent study systematically investi- gated the influence of critical printing parameters for the deliv- ery of bioinks via u-AJP and successfully achieved gelatin line widths down to 20 μm as a model bioink material.[80] In recent years, printing of pure collagen matrices (i.e., without associ- ated gelatin or alginate adjuvants) has also been explored. Gib- ney and Ferraris demonstrated bioprinting of collagen types I and II via AJP to replicate the dense collagenous matter found in the extracellular matrix of connective tissues. Through cir- cular dichroism studies, loss of helicity in the collagen fibers is noted due to ultrasonic exposure and atomization in type I, while type II demonstrated relative invulnerability to the stresses of the AJP process (Figure 10b).[202] In addition, printing dense collagenous type III tissues with suitable mechanical and op- tical properties was also presented for the first time by Gib- ney et al., for the purpose of replicating the cornea for tis- sue engineering applications.[198] Overlapping circular lines of 60 μm in width were printed to form thin layers of collagen type III film. Another area that mer- its the value of AJP in bioink printing is the design and fabri- cation of cost-effective biological test platforms that are neces- sary to eliminate ineffective/toxic therapeutics within the phar- maceutical sector.[203] Mimicking complex microenvironments reminiscent of extracellular matrices has proven challenging and necessitates a manufacturing capability to rapidly screen bioma- terials with high-resolution design flexibility (i.e., rapid iterative patterning). AJP has been explored as an enabling bioprinting process in this endeavor. For instance, Capel et al. investigated AJP for the deposition of controlled microscale patterns of PE- DOT:PSS to create neuronal culture environments on glass as well as poly(potassium 3-sulfopropylmethacrylate) (PKSPMA)- coated glass platforms. [197] These biointerfaces are recognized as excellent candidates that promote cell attachment for up to 96 h without degradation. This demonstration illustrates the value of AJP in the field of bioprinting to produce an organized network of cell guidance designs for in vitro cell culture (e.g., neuronal) studies. Such digitally driven designs further extend the diver- sity of studies achievable under this model to different biological environments. 4.3.2. Tissue Engineering Integration of AJP is realized to be particularly promising for tissue engineering and cell patterning applications (e.g., car- diac repair patches, monitoring cell proliferation of mesenchy- mal cells, nanostructured orthopedic scaffolds) due to its abil- ity to embed living cells conformally in micro- or macrostruc- tures with high resolution and high efficiency. chunks.text: particularly promising for tissue engineering and cell patterning applications (e.g., car- diac repair patches, monitoring cell proliferation of mesenchy- mal cells, nanostructured orthopedic scaffolds) due to its abil- ity to embed living cells conformally in micro- or macrostruc- tures with high resolution and high efficiency. The tissue en- gineering applications of AJP date back to as early as 2006 when Liu and Webster demonstrated scaffolds of poly(lactide- co-glycolide) with dispersed titania nanoparticles for orthope- dic tissue engineering.[204] After seeding the fabricated scaffolds with human osteoblast cells, the authors witnessed an enhanced osteoconductivity and accelerated cellular growth, suggesting that the constructed nanocomposite could successfully mimic the properties of natural bone. With myocardial infarction as the leading cause of death worldwide, Basara et al. mimicked the extracellular matrix and electroconductivity of cardiac tissue through printing a conductive MXene structure on predesigned poly(ethylene glycol) hydrogels using AJP at the cellular reso- lution. The engineered composite design provided topographi- cal and conductive cues for stem cell-derived cardiomyocytes to form the basis of cardiac patches that repair damages follow- ing myocardial infarction injury. MXenes, in particular, have the benefit of cytocompatibility toward the development of conduc- tive biomaterials, and coupled with AJP’s advantages of confor- mal printing, fabricated hybrid tissue constructs are promising alternatives as electroconductive scaffolds for engineering car- diac patches. [71] In addition to the fabrication of cardiac repair patches, other studies have utilized blended inks of conducting polymers (i.e., PEDOT:PSS) and MWCNTs to print (via a combi- nation of IJP and AJP processes) 3D microelectrode arrays (i.e., needle-like electrode tips with diameter = 10 μm and height = 33 μm) that responded to extracellular signals from cardiomyocyte- like HL-1 cells, further endorsing the feasibility of AJP toward the exploration and understanding of cellular electrophysiologi- cal properties. [205] Tonello et al. assembled a low-cost impedance- based approach toward monitoring cell proliferation of human mesenchymal stromal cells using carbon inks AJP deposited onto flexible polyimide substrates. [54] Variations in impedance were compared against outcomes of enzymatic proliferation assays to obtain a noninvasive approach for monitoring scaffold culture systems. 4.3.3. [208,209] Actuators com- posed of a stacked layer of printed silicon (Wacker Elastosil P 7670) and printed with reduced graphene oxide (rGO) electrodes that can withstand maximum elongation of up to 100% have been reported by Reitelshöfer et al. [210,211] Following this ap- proach, recently Martin et al. reported the application of printed DEAs as a functional iris implant that allows focus adjustments with respect to changes in surrounding light conditions.[207] In addition, actuators designed using a similar approach and based on stacked medical grade silicones for applications in Adv. [208,209] Although much work remains in the area of AJP-based actuators, these advancements offer promise toward healthcare solutions where the high energy density and highly dynamic kinematics of DEAs may successfully be applied to conformal wearables and prosthesis. Considering healthcare ap- plications, AJP has also been utilized for mobile eye therapies, [97] cochlear implants, [90] and implantable biosystems. [212] Real-time classification of eye movement through biopotential electrodes offers a therapeutic option to improve the quality of life for those with eye disorders such as convergence insufficiency and strabismus. Mishra et al. introduced a wearable soft electronic system that monitors eye movements via a combination of a vir- tual reality system and skin-like sensing units realized through AJP advances in printing.[97] With over 300 000 cochlear implant users worldwide, advances in miniaturization and large-scale manufacturing methods are needed to address the present demands of handmade manufacturing. Relevant-size microcoil arrays (diameter = 1800 μm) suitable for cochlear implant applications have recently been created through AJP as a proof- of-principle demonstration (Figure 11a,b). Modeling results showed the potential to improve operational spatial resolution with more restrictive spread activation compared to conven- tional cochlear implants. [90] AJP is also utilized as a large-scale manufacturing method of a fully printed, battery-less biosystem capable of monitoring cerebral aneurysm hemodynamics (Fig- ure 11c).[212] In this work, biocompatible silver nanoparticle and polyimide inks were patterned onto soft elastomer substrates for conformal insertions into a biomimetic blood vessel. The wireless flow sensor demonstrated an interrogation distance up to 6 cm when inserted into raw meat. The same research team recently demonstrated a similar implantable system for the real-time monitoring of arterial pressure, pulse rate, and flow that enhanced stent designs through a wireless platform while maintaining conventional mechanics; furthermore, the electronic system was subjected to in vivo rabbit studies as a minimally invasive catheter implant. Electrodiagnostics, an essential subset of modern medical diag- nostics and monitoring, faces issues with typical “wet” electrodes employed in hospital settings and clinics. Considering the push toward dry electrode constructions with significantly enhanced shelf lives, substantial industry research is underway to con- struct such devices, and the benefits of direct-write printing such as compatibility with flexible substrates endow this approach with the capability to manufacture low-cost, lightweight, patient- friendly electrodes. In the investigations by Kwon et al., human– machine interfaces are explored by employing a combination of spin-coating of Kapton onto PMMA/glass substrates and AJP of silver nanoparticle and graphene inks onto elastomeric sub- strates (Figure 11d).[195] Placed directly on the skin, without any conductive gels or external pressure, the fabricated sensor cou- pled with deep learning algorithms displayed recordings of EMG from six

Biorecognition The recognition of biological molecules, particularly at ultralow concentrations, is urgently needed to diagnose and monitor the progression of human disease. In this endeavor, AJP has been recently explored as a technique toward constructing sen- sitive and selective biosensors that detect antibodies, antigens, and neurotransmitters. An ultrasensitive phenylethyl boronic acid-functionalized rGO field-effect transistor was fabricated by AJP on PET for rapid and real-time detection of specific biomolecules.[217] An immunosensor capable of rapid moni- toring of interferon-gamma (IFN-𝛾) and interleukin 10 (IL- 10) cytokines was also demonstrated by printing a graphene- nitrocellulose ink onto polyimide substrates in an IDE pattern.[55] The fabricated devices were highly selective, monitored a wide sensing range (e.g., 0.1–5 ng mL−1 , IFN-𝛾), demonstrated a rapid response time

In parallel work, Cantù et al. ex- ploited the potential of AJP to fabricate an entirely printed electro- chemical sensor for the quantification of interleukin-8 (IL-8) pro- tein. Functionalized with MWCNTs, the sensors demonstrated near commercial-level performance with a LoD as low as 0.3 ng mL−1 .[218] Such biosensors are not only crucial for the early-stage detection of diseases[219–222] and surgical site infections[223] but also for the detection of food-borne pathogens. An example of the latter case was reported by Parate et al. in which a printed graphene-based histamine biosensor was designed for on-site food safety monitoring. Designed for fishery products, the fabri- cated sensors displayed a toxicologically relevant histamine sens- ing range of 6.25–200 ppm and a low detection limit of 3.41 ppm when exposed to real fish broth samples. [116,224] Note that, the minimum histamine toxicity levels (in fish products) rec- ommended by the FDA is 50 ppm to avoid food poisoning and wastage. Due to the rapid advance- ment of printing technology and materials, additively manufac- tured biosensors expand the possibilities of medical diagnostics. In this regard, monitoring of glucose in the clinically relevant range (i.e., 3–10 mm) is particularly important for early diabetes detection and monitoring of cellular processes. As described in the previous section, Yang et al. designed a dual glucose/H 2 O2 sensor utilizing a silver microelectrode array capable of moni- toring catalytic reactions. [180] Glucose oxidase is introduced as a model enzyme to catalyze the oxidation of glucose to H2 O2 , which achieves a high sensitivity (LoD, glucose = 1.7 mm). Tak- ing a noninvasive approach, a semiconductor-based gas sensor for diabetes was microadditively manufactured utilizing SnO2 thin films for acetone vapor detection via breath analysis. [193] Or- ganic electrochemical transistors (OCETs) have also been em- ployed for glucose detection.[104] AJP is utilized to simplify man- ufacturing processes by printing OECTs via four varying func- tionalizations: unfunctionalized device/GOx; PEDOT:PSS/GOx; printed Pt gate/GOx; and sputtered Pt gate/GOx. Printed Pt gate functionalized with GOx exhibited an extensive glucose detec- tion range in phosphate buffer solution (PBS) (i.e., 100 nm–50 mm) and sensitivity to artificial sweat buffer (0.1–10 nm). The same research team has also conducted a follow-on study apply- ing OCETs specifically toward diabetic wound care through de- signing a multivariable (i.e., glucose and temperature) biosens- ing platform and demonstrated in situ monitoring of wound in- fection and healing phases in diabetic mice. [227] Another interest- ing application of AJP-based OCETs for biosensing is the creation of rapid, portable drug testing kits. Following legalization efforts in various territories, reliable detection of the psychoactive com- pound within marijuana (i.e., delta-9-tetrahydrocannabinol (Δ9 - THC)) remains elusive for law enforcement agencies and health- care personnel. Following legalization efforts in various territories, reliable detection of the psychoactive com- pound within marijuana (i.e., delta-9-tetrahydrocannabinol (Δ9 - THC)) remains elusive for law enforcement agencies and health- care personnel. Portable saliva kits that detect Δ9 -THC are a grow- ing interest due to the ease of accurate detection of cannabis intake over other methods such as blood and urine analysis. Majak et al. utilized AJP to design an unfunctionalized OECT, noted for its ability to function well in aqueous media, with a printed PEDOT:PSS as the channel material and printed silver nanoparticles for both source and drain electrodes on polyimide substrates.[196] Although OECTs are rarely used for molecular de- tection, the external Pt wire gate enabled rapid detection (5 min) of Δ9 -THC due to its oxidation–reduction reaction at the gate with devices exhibiting a high sensitivity of detection for a wide range of Δ9 -THC concentration change (0.1 nm–5 mm). In addition to metallic inks, ink formulations based on nanocarbon deriva- tives have also received much attention in the fabrication of ad- vanced biosensors. For example, Goh et al. designed a low-cost, flexible miniaturized chemiresistive pH sensor by printing SWC- NTs into a serpentine-shaped sensing element atop of printed sil- ver electrodes on polyimide. [226] Note that, although detection of pH changes is essential for numerous biomedical (e.g., wound healing [228] ) and environmental processes (e.g. water quality [229] ), pH sensing typically requires a reference electrode which re- stricts device miniaturization. In addition, the rigidity of the pH devices and the risk of electrolyte leakage compound the barriers to integrating pH platforms into wearable sensors. These chal- lenges were surmounted by limiting the device dimensions via AJP with results demonstrating high repeatability, good sensi- tivity, and excellent biocompatibility with murine myoblasts live cells. Utilizing an impedance-based approach, Williams et al. cre- ated a low-cost, handheld blood coagulation test for point-of-care diagnostics via conductive silver inks and SWCNTs printed onto a polyimide platform. [56] The impedance-based biosensor exhib- ited no variation in blood clotting times under the bent state (r = 35

Utilizing an impedance-based approach, Williams et al. cre- ated a low-cost, handheld blood coagulation test for point-of-care diagnostics via conductive silver inks and SWCNTs printed onto a polyimide platform. [56] The impedance-based biosensor exhib- ited no variation in blood clotting times under the bent state (r = 35 mm) and through human blood tests yielded a 70% noise re- duction over commercial potentiostatic devices. Such rapid pro- duction of low-cost portable point-of-care devices with printed sensors can eliminate regular clinic visits resulting in a dra- matic improvement in the quality of life for patients on blood thinners. 4.3.7. Microfluidics In parallel with the emerging wide array of biotechnological applications, the integration of biosensors with a proper mi- crofluidics environment can also revolutionize biological and biomedical research in both academic and industrial platforms. While early microfluidics chips were produced from silicon un- der clean room conditions using expensive and elaborate pho- tolithographic methods, fine chip structures, chambers, and channels can now be produced more economically without ad- ditional assembly steps due to advances in direct-write printing technologies.[230] In this context, AJP has the potential to trans- form the fabrication of microfluidic devices with customized ge- ometries and added functionalities at a rapid pace and reduced material cost. Novo et al. designed and fabricated an electro- chemical microfluidic sensing platform entirely printed by AJP technology for standard enzyme-mediated glucose monitoring, with results showing sensing capability in a clinically relevant range of 3–10 mm.[194] Catic et al. demonstrated the feasibil- ity of AJP for the rapid production of microfluidic molds. [231] Another approach toward manufacturing microfluidics includes a roll-to-roll hot embossing fabrication of microfluidic chan- nels where AJP gold nanoparticles were utilized to manufac- ture high-throughput, highly efficient, and homogenous surface- enhanced Raman spectroscopy (SERS) structures.[232] This study demonstrated the feasibility of AJP-modified fabrication of mi- crofluid SERS chips for quantitative analysis of chemicals and biomolecules. 4.4. During the past few decades, photosensors have been developed for a wide range of wavelengths from infrared (IR) to visible to ultraviolent (UV), which has increased their role in sensing applications. Vis- ible light detectors have been traditionally employed, however, growth in IR- and UV-based technologies has expanded applica- tions in civil and military defense as well as environmental and biological imaging, respectively. Coupled with the advantages of direct-write printing, photosensors may find use as large-area arrays and disposable paper-based modalities. Increasingly, AJP has been applied to the fabrication process (Table 6) to produce devices with next-generational aims using diversified advanced materials as inks and substrates. Traditionally, crystalline in- organic semiconductors are used as the sensing layer in the construction of photosensors. While these materials have some advantages (e.g., Si-based photosensors are the same material as the underlying circuitry allowing for monolithic integration with the electronic readout), they suffer from costly, high-temperature lithography-based fabrication processes

chunks.text: substrates. Traditionally, crystalline in- organic semiconductors are used as the sensing layer in the construction of photosensors. While these materials have some advantages (e.g., Si-based photosensors are the same material as the underlying circuitry allowing for monolithic integration with the electronic readout), they suffer from costly, high-temperature lithography-based fabrication processes that require a rigid, thick active layer and preclude the use of flexible substrates.[233] On the other hand, alternative photosensor materials (e.g., perovskites, organic semiconductors, colloidal quantum dots), which are amenable to the aerosol-jet printing process, have recently attracted interest for their ability to scale into large-area arrays on flexible substrates.[234] The performance of such devices is typi- cally measured via several metrics that are associated with noise, speed, and efficiency; for example, the quantification of photore- sponse strength is termed as the responsivity (ampere/watt (A W−1 )).[234] While the performance of AJP-based devices has been demonstrated to be comparable to[50] or even higher than [74] state-of-the-art, more research is needed to understand how fundamentally defect-free films, and thus optimal performing photodevices, can be unlocked using the advantages of AJP. [75] In addition to being a means toward photodetector fabrication, AJP has also been utilized for photodiode and light-emitting diode constructions, as discussed below. 4.4.1. Photodetectors The first AJP-based organic photodetector was developed by Wang et al. in 2013,[95] in which metalloporphyrin-based nanowire networks of zinc with light-harvesting properties were printed onto PET substrates. The developed prototype demon- strated high photosensitivity as well as fast response and recov- ery times associated with the large surface-to-volume ratio of the nanowires, which facilitates efficient surface-dominated oxygen chemisorption/desorption. On the other hand, Aga et al. used a combination of AJP, inkjet printing, and drop-casting to pro- duce a low-cost polymeric photodetector on a paper substrate. [101] The authors designed these flexible photodetectors by inkjet- printing a silver electrode onto photo paper, followed by AJP de- position of conductive PEDOT:PSS as a subsequent interlayer as well as top electrode where in between AJP of a photoac- tive layer of poly(3-hexylthiophene):C61-butyric acid methyl es- ter blend (P3HT:PCBM) followed by a drop-casted highly trans- parent and

The authors noted that the printed photodetector exhibited a photoresponse in the visible spectrum with two orders of mag- nitude lower responsivity than its commercial Si counterparts. Nevertheless, integrating these printed devices onto paper sub- strates opens a route for designing inexpensive, disposable opti- cal sensors for various applications. Aga et al. also studied specif- ically the thickness of PEDOT:PSS printed on an oxygen plasma- treated Ni electrode for work function modification and demon- strated a threefold increase in the photoresponse of a polymer- based (P3HT:PCBM) Schottky barrier photodetector compared to devices without PEDOT:PSS coatings. [68] AJP technology has also been employed in dichalcogenide-based (e.g., WSe 2 , MoS 2 ) pho- todetectors. For instance, an interesting fully printed CNT/WSe 2 photosensor on flexible polyimide substrates was demonstrated, in which transparent CNT electrodes, rather than opaque metal counterparts, enabled the passage of incident light through the CNT/WSe 2 heterojunction for photocurrent generation. Results showed comparable photoresponsivity in the visible spectrum compared to other flexible photosensors. [42] In another demon- stration, Kuo et al. employed a high frequency megasonic at- omization mode to print MoS 2 -based nanosheet inks atop of graphene electrodes followed by photonic annealing.[73] This combination yielded photodetectors with responsivities of 10 3 A W−1 , representing a three orders of magnitude enhancement than the previously reported all-printed visible light photode- tectors. Photodiodes Early work in AJP-based photodiodes by Eckstein et al. demon- strated the fabrication of inverted configuration semitransparent (device transparency = 15%) organic photodiodes (OPDs).[103] In the work, PET substrates were utilized to construct fully printed flexible organic photodetectors based on a blend of polythieno[3,4-b]-thiophene-co-benzodithiophene (PTB7) and [6,6]-phenyl C71-butyric acid methyl ester (PC70BM) as the light- absorbing layer.[103] The performance of the fabricated semitrans- parent photodetectors was found to be equivalent to state-of-the- art devices constructed on rigid substrates and outperformed pre- viously reported all-printed OPDs without the use of other so- phisticated fabrication processes (i.e., spin-coating, sputtering). Eckstein et al. further developed an OPD array (active area = 250 μm × 300 μm) to produce a 2D image sensor consisting of 256 OPD pixels with high spectral responsivities (0.3 A W −1 ) and specific detectivities (>10 12 Jones) comparable to state- of-the-art inorganic photodiodes (Figure 13a). [236] Near-IR non- fullerene acceptors, namely, IDTBR:P3HT, have been explored by Strobel et al. toward the fabrication of high-performance OPDs with spectral tunability (Figure 13b).[237] Record spectral responsivities are achieved (300 mA W−1 ) in the near-IR, and devices outperform detection speeds of fullerene-based systems by more than an order of magnitude. Notably, the multilay- ered structures of OPDs with different functionalities (e.g., ab- sorption of light, extraction of charges, reduction in detection noise) are challenging to print due to intermixing of materials and disruptions in film morphologies. To this end, the recent work by Seiberlich et al. established an AJP-based method to- ward printing multilayered OPD architectures under the same solvent system. [238] Using a P3HT bulk heterojunction scheme, the authors create a donor blocking layer, without the need for orthogonal solvents or cross linking systems, which spatially ex- tends the donor region of the bulk heterojunction leading to ideal hole extraction and noise reduction via blocking of injected elec- trons. 4.4.3. While LEDs are most commonly used in digital displays or as broadband light sources, they are also utilized in photosensors for diverse applications such as bidirectional communications and ambient light level sensors. Therefore, the application of AJP toward the fabrication of LEDs represents an emerging area of investigation for potential sen- sor integration, and thus, is summarized below. Although some of the earliest reported work with respect to LED manufactur- ing utilized AJP toward the fabrication of direct-write structures as replacements for LED wire bonds,[239,240] more recently, re- searchers have investigated quantum dot (QD)-based technolo- gies that can emit red, green, and blue colors and be incorpo- rated into a micro-LED array.[241,242] Compared to LEDs, organic light-emitting diodes (OLEDs) are significantly thinner, allow- ing them to be multilayered, which leads to brighter output, wider temperature range, and faster response times. [243] Zhou et al. established a low-cost method toward improving OLED performance by printing PEDOT:PSS grids (30 μm width × 100 μm pitch) embedded into the organic layer/ITO interface on the anode surface via AJP. [244] Aside from its demonstration as an anode grid-modifying material, PEDOT:PSS has been uti- lized by other research teams in the advanced manufacturing of AJP-based LED systems.[245] Recently, Hamjah et al. fabricated OLEDs (40 mm 2 active area) on glass substrates using aerosol- jet-printed AgNWs and PEDOT:PSS as bottom electrode and hole transport layers, respectively, in ambient atmosphere. [245] Tait et al. demonstrated the patterning of top-emitting OLEDs, with the archetypical host material poly(N-vinylcarbzole), guest emit- ting dopant complexes (i.e., dopants for red, green, and blue OLEDs), as well as PEDOT:PSS and MoO3 transport layers, all printed via AJP.[246] Active matrix organic light emitting diode displays are generally formed through laminating LED arrays with active matrix TFT backplanes, where the backplane is the biggest cost factor for the display.[247] Manufacturers such as Samsung and LG utilize backplanes consisting of low temper- ature polycrystalline silicon and metal oxides, respectively[248] due to their excellent electrical properties and stabilities. How- ever, TFT backplanes fabricated with polysilicon require vacuum sputtering, lithographic patterning, and acidic etching, which demand high costs in manufacturing, while those based on metal oxides exhibit poor electrical properties in absence of high- temperature annealing, limiting compatible substrates to glass only. Printing of nanocarbon-based materials has offered a low- cost alternative to traditional backplane displays and has been explored by several groups. [247,248] Xu et al. developed a high- yield method to sort semiconducting SWCNTs via wrapping the nanomaterials with a conjugated polymer and then utiliz- ing AJP to fabricate top-gated TFTs on flexible PET substrates. The work by Li et al. produced an all-aerosol-jet-printed SWCNT- based TFT on pixel circuitry LED arrays. [248] Using only AJP, N- electrodes based on gold nanoparticles were first printed followed by insulating polyimide strips; gold nanoparticles were then deposited as TFT drain/source electrodes and SWCNTs were printed into TFT channels as the active layers; finally, polyfluo- rinated resin/EMIM TFSI was printed as dielectric layers and a protective PMMA layer was deposited over the constructed de- vice. 4.5. chunks.text: Emerging Sensor Modalities Owing to its wide range of versatility, AJP technology has ex- panded to a plethora of applications outside of the more com- monly employed fields of strain, gas, and biology to include tem- perature gauges, surface acoustic wave (SAW) sensors, motion detectors, and other sensing mechanisms (Table 7). This sec- tion discusses the novel ways in which AJP has been utilized in other technologies applicable to areas such as smart textiles,[20] smart homes, [22] and smart automotives.[105,249] Such diversity il- lustrates the possible value of AJP as an advanced manufacturing method to produce next-generation bespoke devices with exciting properties. 4.5.1. Surface Acoustic Wave SAW sensors are an exemplary case of emerging sensing modal- ities where the practicality of AJP has recently been explored. By and large, passive SAW devices are built on piezoelectric single crystal substrates and used to access physical properties such as environmental temperature changes. Noting that the SAW propa- gation velocity is affected by temperature variations, by analyzing the time delay between the reflected signals, the SAW transpon- ders’ environmental temperature can be determined. Addition- ally, passive sensing capabilities inherent to SAW sensors make them ideal candidates for areas requiring high temperature or harsh operating conditions where conventional electronics can- not be applied. To avoid conventional complicated lithography processes, Lariviere et al. recently reported the development of an SAW sensor on lithium niobate (LiNbO3 ) substrates at the resolu- tion limit of the aerosol-jet printer (Figure 14b). Designed to func- tion as a temperature as well as electrical resistance gauge, the device displayed higher operating fundamental frequency due to finer printed feature size (i.e., 10 μm silver line widths) compared to previously reported AJP SAW devices. [250] Although most re- ported AJP-based SAW sensors are designed on LiNbO 3[250–252] and lead zirconate titanate (PZT), [253] flexible composites based on resin-impregnated BaTiO3 piezoelectric foams have also been explored (Figure 14a).[254] Aimed at nondestructive structural testing, AJP coupled with laser ablation-based techniques pro- duced silver IDE tracks to generate SAW on a BaTiO 3 /resin com- posite. Despite signal attenuation caused by the resin, displace- ments

[20] Aimed at healthcare applications, both Tiziano et al. [257] and Lim et al.[258] designed flexible temperature sensors on polyimide substrates. The sensors designed by Lim et al. were capable of transmitting body temperatures to a cloud platform for real-time monitoring. Considering that various ap- plication areas (e.g., healthcare, robotics, energy storage) require sensing array solutions to measure temperature distributions across surfaces with high spatial and temporal resolutions, a ther- mistor comprised of high-density sensor pixels (625 pixels on an area of 12 × 12 mm 2 ) has been recently fabricated. This work combined screen printed connection lines together with aerosol- jet printed pixels to produce a sensing matrix capable of operat- ing in the range of 5–90 °C without encapsulation.[259] For SHM and wearable applications, Saeidi-Javash et al. delivered a flexi- ble sensor that simultaneously measured strain and temperature with superior sensitivity (Figure 14c).[70] The bimodal sensor em- ployed an aerosol-jet printed MXene ink for strain measurements based on resistance changes and a printed graphene/MXene ther- mocouple junction for temperature sensing based on differences in their Seebeck coefficients. An improved GF (85% higher than commercial metal strain gauges) and a comparable thermopower output were achieved. Aimed at IoT applications, Stoukatch et al. demonstrated a 3D printed multisensor electronic system that measured, processed, and wirelessly transferred temperature, R H , and light intensity data to a network.[22] AJP can also ad- dress the difficulties associated with the traditional fabrication techniques used to construct 3 omega (3𝜔) sensors for ther- mal conductivity measurements, including high cost and time- consuming methods (e.g., application of mask based and

[260] In this endeavor, Kempf and Zhang demonstrated accurate thermal con- ductivity measurements ranging from 1–150 W m−1 K−1 and up to 300 °C on aluminum nitride and aluminum oxide substrates through AJP printed silver 3𝜔 sensors (Figure 14d). 4.5.3. Automotives AJP-based sensors have recently been employed in applications relevant to automotive safety. Andrews et al. developed capacitive- based printed sensors for tread depth monitoring of automobile tires. In this work, a noninvasive means to probe material thick- ness was demonstrated via exploring various ink formulations (gold nanoparticle, silver nanoparticle, and metallic SWCNTs) printed on glass and polyimide substrates. [59] By measuring the shift in the resonant frequency of a signal propagated between the two printed electrodes due to the attenuation of the electric field by the overlaid material, sensors made of metallic SWCNT ink exhibited the best sensitivity—ten times more sensitive than devices with silver nanoparticle ink. When integrated within the real tire (beneath the tread), the fabricated sensors were able to re- spond to millimetric changes in tire thread depth. Andrews et al. also demonstrated fully printed CNT–TFT pressure sensors ca- pable of detecting pressures ranging from 0 to 42 PSIg.[105] In this work, IoT capabilities of these sensors in smart tire appli- cations were also established via wireless transmittance of sen- sor data over a Bluetooth module. The same group’s latest work provided an adaptation to their previous approach of monitoring tread thickness within a tire by constructing a hybrid Ag-SWCNT sensor array on polyimide positioned against the outside of a tire to measure and map the tread depth profile across the entire width of the tire. [249] 4.5.4. Triboelectric Motion A unique area that merits the application of AJP to sensing is triboelectric motion sensors. Motion sensing is essential in sec- tors such as manufacturing, mapping, transportation, medicine, and robotics. Printed triboelectric motion sensors, relying on the triboelectric charging effect whereby two dissimilar materi- als become electrically charged after coming into contact with another, are typically limited by poor spatial and temporal res- olutions because conventional techniques cannot attain required line widths. Achieving flexible and transparent triboelectric sen- sors has also been challenging as polymers cannot be easily pat- terned into fine features compared to their traditional metallic counterparts. Jing et al. utilized AJP to overcome these barriers to fabricate sensors by printing silver electrodes and polyimide and polyvinylidene difluoride-trifluoroethylene inks with 25 μm line width grated structures resulting in a 50 μm spatial resolu- tion motion sensor that enables detection of speeds ranging from 50 to 300 μm s−1 (Figure 14e). [261] 4.5.5. Environmental Contaminants Following the development of portable handheld Raman spec- trometers, SERS substrates that are amenable to point-of-care sensing capabilities have become increasingly attractive for appli- cations in forensics and trace detection of explosives or environ- mental contaminants. Through AM techniques, the plasmonic enhancement effect in SERS (i.e., increased Raman signals asso- ciated with the excitation of surface plasmons in metal particles following analyte absorption) can be effectively maximized via in- tricate geometries. With these considerations in mind, via AJP McDonnell et al. recently fabricated SERS-based substrates by de- positing graphene and silver nanoparticle inks on polyimide.[262] Using these SERS sensors, detection of environmentally perva- sive pollutants (i.e., perfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS)) has been achieved at concentration levels as low as 0.4 ng L−1 , much lower than the trace detection values defined by the U.S. Environmental Pollution Agency (70 ng L−1 ).[262] 5. Challenges While many innovations have been achieved that show the ex- citing potential of AJP for a variety of applications, further ad- vances in science and engineering are required to meet the chal- lenges of widespread deployment of AJP-based sensing devices. These challenges mainly center around the formulation of inks with the proper viscosity and functionality, selection of suitable substrates possessing mechanical integrity under the processing protocols, compatibility with the deposited inks and the device type, and manufacturing challenges stemming from resolution Adv. Mater. Technol. 2023, 8, 2300030 © 2023 Wiley-VCH GmbH 2300030 (27 of 37) -- 27 of 37 -- www.advancedsciencenews.com www.advmattechnol.de limits, yield, and variability. Considering the shift in focus from hard material platforms to soft polymeric substrates, the lower Tg of common polymers presents barriers to the development of high-quality prints, hence high-performance devices, because ef- fective sintering of conductive inks often requires high tempera- tures above T g that are detrimental to the underlying substrates. To lower the required sintering temperature and the associated energy budget, intense pulse photonic sintering methods em- ploying flash lamps or pulsed lasers enable fast and efficient sin- tering of the printed patterns without damaging the temperature- sensitive polymeric substrates. Because of their low surface en- ergy (i.e., hydrophobicity), another challenge stems from efficient distribution and adhesion of the inks to the polymeric substrates. This challenge requires additional surface treatment steps (e.g., chemical modification, mechanical roughening, plasma treat- ment, etc.) to increase the surface energy, hence wettability of the polymer, but at the expense of increased processing complex- ity and manufacturing cost. [263] Further challenge is associated with the reliability in sustaining the properties of printed inks on polymers when deformed or stretched, which can be circum- vented by developing more intrinsically flexible and stretchable inks with specific additives. [264] Considering biosensors, the bio- compatibility of the substrate is another primary concern, where priming steps

[264] Considering biosensors, the bio- compatibility of the substrate is another primary concern, where priming steps and immobilization techniques are often needed in substrate preparation to adhere biological agents to the rele- vant surface. For the case on woven textiles, printed sensors face issues associated with the homogeneity and density of printed features on curved surfaces of fibers and porous structures of wo- ven materials. [20,125] Other limitations of AJP techniques include high resistivity of printed patterns and feature size limitations due to material over- spray. When droplets exit the deposition head by way of the car- rier gas, smaller diameter droplets are often carried away by the deposition axis by the sheath gas exiting the nozzle jet. This dis- tribution of droplet sizes accordingly results in a line that has a dense core region surrounded by a diffuse area of overspray.[32] Overspray as an inherent feature of AJP is defined as deposi- tion of the smallest aerosol droplets outside the intended pattern. High resistivity usually results from the residual chemicals (i.e., surfactants, stabilizers) added to the ink formulation. While opti- mization of sheath gas or atomizer flow rate can minimize over- spray, it cannot completely eliminate this particular issue. Espe- cially for printed microelectronics and sensor applications, mini- mization of overspraying is a key metric for print quality control. In fact, Optomec has recently performed a metrological study to understand the underlying physical mechanisms leading to over- spray and now offers a quantification method toward evaluating its severity. [265] They concluded that the amount of overspraying can be attenuated by increasing jet velocity and sheath-to-mist ratio and becomes negligible when the distance is beyond 30– 40% of line width (i.e., width of the printed line pattern) from the line edges (i.e., edges of the printed line). In another study, a 3D computational fluid dynamics model of aerosol carrier gas flow (i.e., confined by annular sheath gas flow) has been devel- oped to explain the fundamental fluid mechanics from which overspray originates as a function of sheath gas flow and droplet size distribution.[266] It was concluded that there exists an inter- play between different gas flow rates and size of the ink parti- cles that dictates the width of a printed line and the resulting overspray phenomenon; and to achieve a good print resolution and for minimized overspray, optimization of AJP operating pa- rameters (e.g., nozzle exit diameter, size distribution of droplets within the aerosol, and carrier gas flow rate) will be needed. Par- allel to this effort, hybrid machine learning methods are also be- ing implemented to determine optimal adjustable print process- ing parameters (e.g., sheath gas flow rate, carrier gas flow rate, and print speed) with respect to printed line quality, resulting in fabricated lines with improved edge definitions and attenu- ated overspray.[267] Although more studies are needed on other design dimensions, including ink rheologies, standoff distance, and temperature of the substrates during operation for a com- plete picture of design principles, machine learning methods help to revolutionize the manufacturing process toward meeting the demands of tomorrow’s electronics. In addition to the ongoing efforts toward solving the chal- lenges outlined above, in many instances, increasing sensitivity, selectivity, and stability of the sensor response remains a signifi- cant challenge requiring coordinated efforts to develop new ma- terial combinations, chemistries, and device architectures to sat- isfy the requirements imposed by the nature of the final applica- tion. For example, the integration of microheaters for gas sensing applications increases complexity of the manufacturing process and presents complications for temperature-sensitive platforms. Accordingly, when used in real settings, dynamic environmen- tal factors such as humidity and temperature increase issues re- lated to selectivity metrics by altering association and dissociation

For example, the integration of microheaters for gas sensing applications increases complexity of the manufacturing process and presents complications for temperature-sensitive platforms. Accordingly, when used in real settings, dynamic environmen- tal factors such as humidity and temperature increase issues re- lated to selectivity metrics by altering association and dissociation rate constants and affecting accompanying binding interactions between the active layer and analyte. While AJP can effectively increase manufacturing throughput by reducing dual-step print- ing processes to a single technique (e.g., screen followed by inkjet printing), at large-scale or roll-to-roll manufacturing levels, main- taining the print accuracy and improving production yield and throughput are not trivial tasks. In fact, at high-batch commercial production scales, AJP is inherently prone to nonlinear gradual drifts in material transport and deposition that could potentially result in batch-to-batch variabilities. Accordingly, quality inspec- tion standards for high-volume and low-volume production must be defined to realize commercial viability. Another important re- quirement is related to the device form factor that requires fur- ther advances in understanding the underlying mechanisms that dictate high-resolution printing processes to downscale the de- vice footprint for integration into and interfacing with more com- plex systems and structures. Moreover, reliability can prove to be difficult to achieve in production environments where frequent replacement of inks may be required.[35] Hence, real-time process monitoring and closed-loop controls are needed to quantify the influence of printing parameters on device reproducibility. [268,269] 6. Direct-write printing has been widely adopted in sensor fabrica- tion due to readily accessible simplified printing methods and the availability of diverse raw material choices for practical print designs.
